events.text: Chuseok night, and the moon as round as a rice cake. The young people of the village have made a turtle out of sorghum leaves, a great rustling hump with a head on a stick, and this year you are the one inside it, crawling from yard to yard with the drums and gongs behind you, blessing each house with long life in exchange for rice cakes. At the old stone well the drummers stop to drink. You put your head out of the sorghum turtle and look down the well, and something looks up at you: a real turtle, black, the size of a winnowing tray, sitting on a ledge just above the water, with a black snake wound round its shell. Both heads are looking at you.

choices.text: Drop it a rice cake from the turtle's takings

effects.log: You take the best rice cake from the basket, the half-moon one with sesame inside, and drop it down the well. The snake takes it before it reaches the water, quick as a word. The tortoise does not move. It goes on looking at you with two small dark eyes, slowly, the way an old person looks at a child they have decided to remember. When the drummers call, you crawl on, and all night you feel lighter, as if you had been blessed instead of doing the blessing.

choices.text: Sing the children's song down the well: "Turtle, turtle, put forth your head"

effects.log: "Turtle, turtle, put forth your head," you sing down the well, the way the children sing it to the river turtles, "or we will roast you and eat you." Both heads go in at once. Then, very slowly, one comes out: the snake's, with an air of having been insulted. Then, slower still, the other: the tortoise's, with an air of having been asked politely. They look at each other. They look at you. You laugh out loud inside the sorghum turtle, and the drummers ask what is so funny, and you cannot explain it.

choices.text: Climb down, lift it out, and carry it to the river inside the sorghum turtle

ok.log: It is heavier than a sack of rice and colder than the well. The snake winds once round your wrist and stays there, not biting, while you carry the tortoise down to the river under the sorghum leaves, and the drummers follow thinking it is part of the play. At the water you set it down. It walks in without hurry. The snake unwinds from your wrist last of all, and at the edge of the water both heads turn and look back at you, together, once.

fail.log: You get it out of the well and drop it twice on the way to the river, and the second time the snake bites you on the thumb, not hard, more as a remark. At the water the tortoise walks in without hurry. Your thumb throbs until the New Year, and in a strange way you are proud of it. (-6 health)

events.text: {npc}, a diviner of the court, pays well and asks few questions: a hundred taels for a hundred-year shell, for the brazier where the kingdom's fortunes are read in the cracks. "A black one," {npc} says. "There is one in the cold river under the northern ford. The fishermen will not net it." You find it on the third night, in the shallows under the ice-rimmed reeds: a black tortoise the size of a winnowing tray, with a black snake wound round its shell. Before you can put your hands on it, the snake lifts its head out of the water and speaks to you in a human voice, dry and quick. "A bargain," it says. "Let us go, and I will read your future in this river. Truly. I never lie about the future. Only about the past."

choices.text: Take the tortoise to {npc}'s brazier

effects.log: You wrap it in a wet sack and carry it south, and the snake says nothing at all the whole way, which is worse than anything it could have said. {npc} pays fifty taels in advance and sets it in a stone tank behind the brazier hall. In the morning the tank is empty. There is a shed snake skin lying in it, whole, folded neatly as a letter, and on the wet stone the print of a shell, as if something heavy had sat there a long time thinking before it left.

choices.text: Take the snake's bargain

effects.log: The snake looks into the black water between the reeds for a long time, and the tortoise waits beside it the way a stone waits. "In the year the first white comes into your hair," the snake says at last, "you will stand on a bridge that is not there, and you will not fall." Then they are gone under the ice. You go back to {npc} with empty hands and say the river was empty. {npc} looks at your face for a long moment, and does not ask again.

choices.text: Bring {npc} an ordinary river turtle and swear it is a hundred years old

ok.log: You buy a brown turtle from a boy at the ford for a handful of coppers, rub its shell with soot and lamp oil until it shines, and swear to {npc} on your ancestors. {npc} pays thirty taels. In the reeds behind you, as you leave the river, you hear something that might be a snake laughing.

fail.log: {npc} turns the turtle over, scrapes the soot off its belly with one fingernail, and hands it back to you without a word. You let it go at the ford. Somewhere under the ice, you are fairly sure, a black tortoise and a black snake are discussing you.

events.text: Winter solstice, the longest night. The seven mansions of the northern sky, Dipper and Ox, Girl and Emptiness, Rooftop, Encampment and Wall, come down one after another and are a tortoise and a snake made of stars. They settle on the frozen river below your hall, a shell as wide as the ice is long, and every well in the district skins over at once. "The council of the four directions," says the tortoise, slowly, "has had no clerk," says the snake, quickly, "for a very long time," they say together, "and the Bird burns the minutes." They want a human strong enough to be heard in heaven to keep the record of one hearing. A kingdom has fallen. Its guardian, a great grey crane of the old mountains, stands in the frost before you and says it could not have been saved. The brush is in your hand.

choices.text: Write the tortoise's account: what was seen

effects.log: You write what happened and nothing else: the harvest that failed, the granaries that stayed shut, the night the gate was opened from inside, the crane on the wall watching. You do not write why. When you finish, the tortoise reads it over with its head close to the page, as slow as frost growing, and nods once. "Seen," it says. The snake, for once, says nothing, and it is the loudest nothing you have ever heard.

choices.text: Write the snake's account: what was meant

effects.log: You write what everyone meant: the minister who shut the granaries to save them for a worse year, the captain who opened the gate to spare the city a siege, the crane who meant to warn the king and waited one day too long. When you finish, the snake reads it in one quick glance and laughs. "Meant," it says. "Nobody ever writes that down. It is the only part that explains anything." The tortoise blinks, very slowly, which in a tortoise is a frown.

choices.text: Write both accounts side by side, in two columns

ok.log: Two columns down the paper: on the right what was seen, on the left what was meant, line by line, the gate and the captain, the granary and the minister, until the two columns meet at the bottom of the sheet in one sentence that belongs to both. The tortoise and the snake read it at the same time, heads together, and for the first time that night they do not finish each other's sentences. They simply agree. The crane bows to you. The stars come apart and go back up into the north.

fail.log: You try to keep two columns and they run into each other halfway down the sheet, the gate in the wrong column, the minister's reason under the wrong night. Your head aches as if two people were talking into it at once. The tortoise and the snake read it together and, after a long silence, say together: "Honest, at least." (-8 health)

events.text: A year after the solstice hearing, a snow goose lands in your courtyard at dawn, walks up to your door as if it owned the house, and drops at your feet a thin black plate like a slice of slate. Scratched into it, very small and very neat, is your record of the hearing, every word. Under it, in two different hands, one slow and square and one quick and slanting, someone has added a single line.

choices.text: Read the line in the slow, square hand

effects.log: "Filed in the north," it says, "under Emptiness, with the endings of kingdoms. Kept." You find you are glad, the way you are glad when a grave is properly tended. You keep the slate on your desk. On winter nights it is colder than the room, and steadier.

choices.text: Read the line in the quick, slanting hand

effects.log: "The Bird tried to burn it," it says. "I bit the Bird. Not hard. Thank you for the work." You laugh until the goose looks offended. You keep the slate. Once, years later, it is warm for a whole day, and you hear a rumour of a quarrel in heaven.

choices.text: Give the slate back to the goose to carry north

effects.log: The goose takes it in its beak with enormous dignity and flies north. You have the odd feeling that you have passed a test you did not know you were taking: the record was never yours to keep.

events.text: {npc}, an archivist of the Northern Palace in robes the colour of deep water, finds you in the Upper Realm carrying a box of black lacquer. "Your record of the hearing has been shelved," {npc} says, "in the Hall of the Wall, where heaven keeps its secret books. The Black Tortoise asks whether you would keep one more record. The snake asks whether you would keep it a little faster."

choices.text: Keep one more record

effects.log: One more hearing, one more winter: a city drowned when a dyke failed, and the river god who says the dyke was never the river god's to hold. You write it as you wrote the first. At the end the tortoise touches the page with one cold foot, and the snake touches it with its tongue, and the record goes into the box of black lacquer under your name.

choices.text: Tell {npc} that once was enough

effects.log: {npc} writes your refusal down too, carefully, in the same box. "Refusals are records," {npc} says. "Most clerks forget that." Far off in the Northern Palace a deep voice and a quick one laugh at the same time.

events.text: The eighth day of the fourth month, Buddha's Birthday, and the road to the temple is hung with lotus lanterns. At the bottom of the temple steps a peddler sells living things to be set free for merit: sparrows in wicker, carp in a tub, turtles in a flat basket. Most of the turtles are brown and sleepy. One is black and no bigger than your palm, and round its shell, like a thread round a spool, is wound a tiny black snake. Both heads are watching you.

choices.text: Buy it with your festival coins and carry it to the river

effects.log: Every coin you had for sweets. The peddler counts them twice and drops the little black thing into your cupped hands, cold as a pebble. You carry it to the river below the temple instead of the pond, because the pond is crowded, and set it in the shallows. It does not hurry off like the others. It turns round, both heads, and looks at you, and then it walks into the deep water as if it knew exactly where it was going.

choices.text: Write a character on its shell with soot from a lantern

effects.log: You dip your finger in the lantern soot and write on its back the only character you know properly, the one for long life, crooked. The peddler laughs. The snake watches your finger the whole time, very closely, as if it were learning to write. When you look back from the temple steps the soot has not smudged at all, though the basket is wet.

choices.text: Hold one finger out to the snake

effects.log: The tiny snake looks at your finger for a long time. Then it touches it with its tongue, once, as light as a hair. The tortoise head comes out and looks at the snake, and you could swear it is scolding it. The peddler says nobody has ever been licked by that one; it bites everybody. You go home feeling as if you had been told a secret.

events.text: The Chuseok after the night at the well, you drop a rice cake down it again, half as a joke. In the morning the bucket comes up with something in it that was not there when it went down: a smooth black river stone, perfectly round, wet and very cold, of a kind there is no river near enough to come from.
events.arc: The Rice Cake in the Well

choices.text: Keep the stone under your pillow

effects.log: It stays cold all year, even in the hottest nights of summer. You sleep on it and dream of deep water, of a slow voice and a quick one arguing about the best way upstream. You wake rested every morning, which in your house is a miracle.

choices.text: Drop a second rice cake down the well

effects.log: The second one goes down and does not splash, as if it had been caught. After that, every Chuseok, a rice cake goes down the well from you, and every Chuseok a stone comes up. You have quite a pile by the time you are grown.

choices.text: Tell the village the well has a guardian

effects.log: The village decides you are a liar and then, a year later, decides you were right, because the well never once runs dry in the drought that ruins every other well in the valley.

events.text: Market day in the county town. A peddler has a flat basket of turtles for the temple-goers to buy and set free, and in the corner, half under the others, is one you know: black, small, and wound round with a black snake. It has been caught somehow. When it sees you, both heads come out at once.
events.arc: The Rice Cake in the Well

choices.text: Buy it, whatever the price, and carry it to the temple pond (5 taels)

effects.log: Five taels, which the peddler doubles when he sees your face. You carry it up the temple road in both hands. A monk is chanting over the pond, the long sutra for the creatures set free. You set it on a lotus pad. It sits there in the morning sun looking at you as if you had been late.

choices.text: Argue the peddler down with the old proverb about merit

ok.log: "A turtle sold for merit three times," you say loudly, "is merit for nobody," and the other buyers mutter, and the peddler gives it to you for a copper to make you go away. You let it go in the river, not the pond. The river is where it was going.

fail.log: The peddler will not move on the price and you do not have it. You come back at dusk with the money borrowed from a neighbour and the basket is empty: every turtle sold. Except that under the empty basket, on the wet ground, is a smooth black river stone.

choices.text: Walk on: it can look after itself

effects.log: You walk on. That night you dream of a basket, and of a snake that bites the peddler's thumb, and of a turtle that walks out across the market while everybody is shouting. In the morning the peddler is at the inn with a bandaged thumb, telling everyone about it.

events.text: Years later you are old enough that the young people of the village now make the sorghum turtle without you. On Chuseok night you stand at the old well while they drink, and look down. The ledge above the water is empty, and has been for years. On it, wet and round, sits one black stone.
events.arc: The Rice Cake in the Well

choices.text: Drop one last rice cake, for old times

effects.log: It falls into the dark and does not splash. Far away, somewhere north, you are sure of it, a slow head and a quick one look up at the same moment, as if somebody had called their name.

choices.text: Tell the young ones what used to sit on the ledge

effects.log: They do not believe you, of course. But next Chuseok one of them drops a rice cake down the well, and the year after that it has become a custom, and nobody remembers who started it. You do.

events.text: Since the Chuseok when you sang down the well, you have fallen into a habit you cannot explain: in the evenings you walk up to the temple pond and sit on the flat stone at its edge and talk. About the day. About the price of salt, the neighbour's quarrel, the thing you should have said. Nobody answers. But every evening, a little after you start, two small ripples come across the pond toward your stone, side by side, and stop.

choices.text: Keep talking, every evening

effects.log: You talk, and the two ripples listen. In a year you find you have said things to that pond you have never said to a living person, and that you are kinder at home, as if the pond had taken the sharp edge off you and kept it.

choices.text: Sing them the song again, softly

effects.log: "Turtle, turtle, put forth your head." Two heads come up out of the green water side by side: the slow one, then the quick one, the same order as at the well. The monk sweeping the steps stops and stares. You nod to him, as if this were quite ordinary, and he nods back.

choices.text: Stop going: people will talk

effects.log: You stop. The neighbours stop talking about you, and you find you miss being talked about less than you miss the pond.

events.text: Years of evenings at the pond. Your knees are bad now and the walk up to the temple takes twice as long. Tonight, when you sit down on the flat stone, the ripples come as always, and then, for the first time in all those years, the pond answers. The voice is quick and dry, and comes from a little black head on a long neck. "You never finished the story," it says, "about the neighbour's ox."

choices.text: Finish the story about the ox

effects.log: So you finish it, the whole stupid affair of the neighbour's ox and the magistrate's cabbage, and the snake laughs so hard it has to hold on to the tortoise's shell. The tortoise only blinks. But it does not go under until you have finished, and when you stand up to go it puts its head out, slowly, and touches your foot with its nose.

choices.text: Ask it why it never spoke before

effects.log: "I did not know how," the snake says. "A storyteller taught me. Under a bridge. But the tortoise said we should listen first. All those years of listening." It sounds aggrieved. "The tortoise is very patient." From under the water a slow bubble rises, which might be agreement.

events.text: You are very old, and you know you will not make the walk to the pond many more times. You have one thing left to say that is not for the pond: a word for somebody who will come after you, a person you will not live to meet, about where the family's seed rice is hidden and why the eldest line quarrelled with the youngest forty years ago.

choices.text: Give the word to the pond to keep

effects.log: You say it to the water slowly, twice. The snake repeats it back to you, word for word, and then the tortoise, slower, word for word again. "Kept," they say together. You walk home lighter than you have walked in years.

choices.text: Write it down instead, the human way

effects.log: You write it on good paper and fold it into the family register. Paper burns, the snake would say. But you feel a hand of cold pond water on your shoulder that night, as if something approved of your trying.

events.text: The summer floods come down the valley brown and fast, and you are caught on the river in a borrowed boat with a neighbour's sick child and a jar of medicine. Halfway across, the current takes the boat broadside. Then, from underneath, something lifts it: a broad, slow, steady push, like a hand under a tray, and the boat goes level and straight across to the far bank as if the river had been told to behave.

choices.text: Lean over and look into the water

effects.log: Through the brown water, for an instant, a black shell as wide as the boat, and a thin black head turned up toward you, and then only flood. You deliver the medicine. The child lives. You do not tell the neighbour how.

choices.text: Say thank you out loud, to the river

effects.log: "Thank you," you say to the brown water, feeling foolish, and something under the boat knocks once on the planks, gently, like a knuckle on a door. On the bank the child asks who you were talking to. "An old friend," you say, and are surprised to find it true.

events.text: Every flood since, the same: whenever you are on the river in high water, the boat goes level. The ferry people have noticed. They have started asking you to cross with them in the bad months, the way sailors carry a lucky cat, and the ferry master wants to pay you a share.

choices.text: Ride with them, for nothing

effects.log: You ride every flood crossing for three summers, and no boat with you in it goes over. You never take a copper. On the last crossing of the third summer, the push from beneath comes twice, slow and then quick, like two hands, and you understand you are being thanked as well.

choices.text: Take the ferry master's share

effects.log: Twelve taels a summer. The boats stay level. But the push from beneath is a little later every time, a little grudging, and in the third summer it does not come at all, and you have to swim for it.

choices.text: Tell them it is not you, it is the river, and they should thank it

effects.log: The ferry people start dropping a handful of rice into the river before every flood crossing. It costs them nothing. The boats stay level whether you are in them or not. You think the river likes being thanked.

events.text: Playing at the ford with the other children, you turn over a flat stone and there, sitting under it in the cold water, is a small black turtle with a black snake wound round it. It is a little bigger than it was on Buddha's Birthday. The others shriek and reach for sticks.

choices.text: Stand in front of it with your arms out

effects.log: You stand in the water with your arms out like a gatekeeper until the others get bored and go to catch frogs instead. When you look down, the turtle is gone, and on the flat stone, perfectly dry in the middle of the wet, is the print of a small shell.

choices.text: Show them the trick of singing it out

effects.log: "Turtle, turtle, put forth your head," you sing, and the others join in, and both heads come out, one after the other, and every child at the ford falls silent with delight. Nobody reaches for a stick again. By summer it is a game: whoever finds it sings, and nobody is allowed to touch.

events.text: Grown, you cross a cold river in the north on some errand, and on a rock in the middle of the ford sits a black tortoise the size of a winnowing tray, with a black snake round its shell. On its back, faded but clear after all these years, is a sooty character for long life, crooked, in a child's hand.

choices.text: Wade out to it

effects.log: It waits for you. Up close the character is not soot any more: it has grown into the plate, the way a name cut in a young tree grows with the bark. The snake touches your hand with its tongue, the way it did when you were small. You stand in the cold ford until your feet are numb, and do not mind.

choices.text: Bow from the bank and go on

effects.log: You bow. Both heads bow back, or seem to. All the way across the ford the water is warmer than it should be, and at the far side you find you are smiling, and that the errand goes better than it had any right to.

events.text: {npc} the diviner sends for you. The fifty taels, it seems, were paid for a shell that walked out of a locked hall. {npc} does not want the money back. {npc} wants to know what you saw at the river, exactly, every word, because since that night every plastron in the brazier has cracked in the same pattern: two lines wound round each other, like a snake round a shell.

choices.text: Tell {npc} the whole truth, the bargain you refused

effects.log: {npc} listens without moving, and at the end says only: "It offered you the future and you sold it for fifty taels." Not unkindly. "So did I, once." The next morning the brazier cracks clean and ordinary again, and {npc} looks ten years older and somehow relieved.

choices.text: Say you saw nothing but a turtle

effects.log: {npc} nods slowly and lets you go. For a year after that, every time you pass a well, you hear, faintly, two voices talking quietly about you at the bottom of it.

choices.text: Return the fifty taels anyway (50 taels)

effects.log: {npc} takes the silver and drops it, all of it, into the brazier, where it hisses and runs. "An offering," {npc} says, "to whatever walked out of my tank." That night the plastron cracks in one long straight line from north to south, which in the old books means a debt paid.

events.text: Years later you hear that a black tortoise has been taken at last, at the northern ford, by a sect that wants its shell for the brazier, and is kept in a cage of iron reeds in their hall. Nobody has told you this on purpose. You have heard it three times in one week, in three different towns, as if the news were looking for you.

choices.text: Go and break the cage

ok.log: It is a short fight in a dark hall. The cage is iron; your hands are stronger. The tortoise walks out without hurry, and the snake, passing you, says in its dry quick voice: "Fifty taels. Now we are even." You laugh all the way home with a cut across your cheek.

fail.log: The sect's guards are better than you hoped. But in the fight somebody kicks over the brazier, and in the smoke and the shouting the cage is found open and empty, and nobody knows who opened it. Perhaps nobody did. (-16 health)

choices.text: Pay the sect for it and carry it north yourself (80 taels)

effects.log: Eighty taels. A month's slow walk north with a heavy sack. At the ford you set it down. Before it goes in, the snake says, "You have learned something." The tortoise says nothing, but it turns and looks at you for a long time before the water closes over it.

choices.text: Let the news pass: it walked out once, it can again

effects.log: It does. You hear in the spring that the sect's hall was found one morning with its cage open and every plastron in its brazier cracked into the same picture: two heads facing each other. The sect moved south and does not talk about it.

events.text: It is the year the first white comes into your hair, and you have half forgotten the snake's words at the river. You are crossing a gorge at night on a rope bridge in a storm when the ropes part, all of them, at once. The bridge is not there. Your feet are standing on something broad and wet and cold and steady, in the middle of the air over the torrent, and you do not fall.
events.arc: A Bridge That Is Not There

choices.text: Walk on across, not looking down

effects.log: Twenty steps over the dark, each one landing on something that is there when your foot comes down and gone when it lifts. On the far side you sit down on the rock and shake until dawn. When you look back, there is nothing over the gorge but rain, and below, in the torrent, for one moment, the dark backs of a great many turtles sinking.

choices.text: Look down

ok.log: You look down, and see: fish and turtles, a hundred of them, a thousand, backs together, a bridge made of their backs, and in the middle, under your feet, one black shell with a snake round it. The snake looks up at you and says, quite clearly over the storm: "I told you. I never lie about the future." Then you are across, and they are gone.

fail.log: You look down and see nothing at all, only the torrent and the dark, and your knees go, and you crawl the rest of the way on something you cannot see. You do not fall. That was the promise. It did not say you would be dignified about it. (-8 health)

events.text: {npc}, the diviner who once sent you north for a shell, is royal diviner now, old and grave, and asks you to supper. Over the wine {npc} asks, very quietly, the one question {npc} has never been able to ask anyone else: "At the river. Did the snake keep its word?"
events.arc: A Bridge That Is Not There

choices.text: Tell {npc} about the bridge that was not there

effects.log: {npc} listens with both hands round the cup. "Then it is true," {npc} says at last. "Forty years I have read the future in shells that were dead. And there is one that is alive, and reads truly, and keeps its word." {npc} sets down the cup. "I will never put a living shell in the brazier again."

choices.text: Say it is not yours to tell

effects.log: {npc} smiles, the first smile you have seen on that grave face. "That is an answer too," {npc} says. "A diviner learns to read silence." You part as friends. In the spring, you hear, the royal diviner had the turtle tanks of the court emptied into the river.

events.text: Your sooty brown turtle has had a career. You hear it at an inn: the court diviner's new hundred-year shell was heated at the New Year and read for the kingdom, and the cracks said a dry spring. The court has ordered the farmers to plant millet instead of rice. The farmers in your valley are already digging up their seedbeds.

choices.text: Go to the court and confess

ok.log: It takes nine days to be let in and nine minutes to say it. The diviner goes white, then red. The order about the millet is quietly withdrawn "after further reading". You are beaten for it, but not badly, and the spring is wet.

fail.log: Nobody will hear a confession that makes the court look foolish. You are beaten at the gate and sent home. But somebody did hear: the order about the millet is withdrawn a month later, without a reason given. (-12 health)

choices.text: Tell the farmers in your valley to plant rice anyway

effects.log: Half of them listen. The spring is wet. The half that planted rice eat well and look at you strangely for the rest of your life, as if you might be a diviner yourself.

choices.text: Keep your head down

effects.log: The spring is wet. The millet drowns. You are not the only liar in the kingdom, but for that one year, in your valley, you feel like it.

events.text: On a winter morning there is a black plate of shell on your doorstep, as big as your palm, hexagonal, split down the middle by one clean crack. Somebody has scratched characters into the two halves. On one: what you did. On the other: what you meant. They do not quite fit back together.

choices.text: Keep it, as a lesson

effects.log: You keep the two halves on your desk. Some days they seem a little closer together than others. On the day you finally tell the whole story aloud to someone, they touch.

choices.text: Carry it back to the northern ford and leave it on the ice

effects.log: A month north. On the ice at the ford you set the two halves down side by side. In the morning they are gone, and in their place, frozen into the ice, is a print: a shell, and beside it, a thin curving line that might be a snake, or might be a signature.

events.text: Since the solstice hearing you notice things ending. Not more than before: you simply see them now, the way a clerk sees mistakes. The last kiln of a pottery village going cold. An old ferry's last crossing. A family's last harvest from the field it has farmed for nine generations. Each time you feel the brush in your hand, though there is no brush.

choices.text: Write each ending down, plainly, as you saw it

effects.log: A book of endings, one page each: the kiln, the ferry, the field. Nothing about why. You find, oddly, that writing them down makes them bearable. On the solstice the book is lying open on your desk, and the page you wrote last is rimed with frost in the shape of a nod.

choices.text: Stop seeing them: that was one night's work

effects.log: You put it out of your mind. But in the north, on the longest night, you are sure the tortoise is looking at a blank page with your name at the top, and being patient about it.

events.text: A voice in your ear at a banquet, dry and quick, that no one else at the table hears: "Watch the minister on the left. He means to resign tomorrow, and nobody will ever know why but us." You know that voice. Since you wrote down what was meant, the snake has been dropping in.

choices.text: Ask the snake why he means to resign

effects.log: "Because he was right," the snake says, "and it was not enough." You watch the minister all evening. He laughs and toasts and goes home early, and the next morning he is gone, and you are the only one in the capital who does not need to wonder.

choices.text: Tell it to go home to the tortoise

effects.log: "I am home," the snake says, offended. "I am round it. It is round me. It is very complicated." But it goes. You miss the gossip for a year, which you would admit to nobody.

events.text: The grey crane whose kingdom you recorded lands in your courtyard on a winter dawn, older than it was, and folds its long legs under it on the frozen stones. "I have read your two columns every winter for years," it says. "The left one forgives me. The right one does not. I have decided they are both correct."

choices.text: Ask it what it will do now

effects.log: "Guard something smaller," the crane says. "A village. A well. Something I can see all of at once." It flies off south the next morning. Years later you hear of a village where no child has drowned in living memory, and a crane that stands in its fields.

choices.text: Make it tea and say nothing

effects.log: You make tea. The crane drinks it delicately, the way cranes do everything, and the two of you sit in the cold courtyard until the sun is up, not talking, the way people sit after a funeral when the talking is done.

events.text: Buddha's Birthday. The whole town carries baskets down to the river to set living things free for merit: carp, loaches, turtles bought from the peddlers at the temple gate. You have saved for a turtle of your own. But walking back along the bank you see, in the reeds downstream, the same peddler who sold it to you, quietly netting the turtles out of the shallows as fast as the town puts them in.

choices.text: Shout it to the whole bank

effects.log: The bank turns as one person. The peddler drops the net and runs, and thirty turtles walk out of it into the river in thirty directions. An old monk claps you on the shoulder and says the merit of it is yours, all thirty. You are not sure merit works like that. You do not argue.

choices.text: Wade in and cut the net

ok.log: You slice the net with a reaping knife and the turtles pour out. The peddler swings at you and slips in the mud. The last turtle out of the net is a small black one you did not see in any basket, with a thread of black snake round it, and it is in no hurry at all.

fail.log: The peddler knocks you into the river and keeps the net. You come up spitting weed. But that night, you hear, the net was found cut through from the inside, as if something with very sharp small teeth had been busy. (-6 health)

choices.text: Buy your turtle back from him and release it upstream

effects.log: He sells it to you a second time without a flicker of shame. You walk it a mile upstream, past every net, and set it in a pool under an alder. It is a small lesson in merit, you think: it is not in the buying, it is in the walking.

events.text: The next Buddha's Birthday the peddler is back at the temple gate with his basket, as if nothing had happened. But this year every turtle in the basket has its head drawn in and will not put it out, and the peddler cannot sell a single one. Sitting on the temple wall above him, enormous and black, is a tortoise you have never seen in your life, with a snake round its shell, watching.

choices.text: Buy the whole basket together with the neighbours, and release them

effects.log: A coin from each house in the lane. The peddler sells the lot at a loss, glad to be rid of them. The moment the basket touches the river, every head comes out. On the temple wall the great black tortoise is gone, and where it sat the stones are wet.

choices.text: Tell the peddler who is watching him

effects.log: He looks up, and goes the colour of rice flour, and walks to the river and empties his own basket into it without a word. You hear he became a ferryman afterwards, and the most careful one on the river.

events.text: A wandering monk stops at your family's gate for alms, looks at your face, and goes very still. Afterwards, when you follow him down the lane to ask why, he tells you plainly, because he is that kind of monk: the lines on your face say you will die at nineteen. Then he says something stranger. "On the mountain behind the village, on the third day of the third month, two old men play baduk on a rock under a pine. Take them wine and dried meat. Serve them. Say nothing until they speak to you."

choices.text: Climb the mountain with wine and dried meat

effects.log: You steal the wine from the family jar and the meat from the rafters and climb at dawn. Near the top, under a twisted pine, there they are: two old men at a board, one with a fair, kind face, one dark and stern. Neither looks up. You kneel and pour.

choices.text: Laugh it off: monks say such things

effects.log: You laugh. But on the third day of the third month you find yourself awake before dawn, with a jar of wine in your hands, standing at the foot of the mountain path, not quite sure how you got there.

events.text: The two old men play on and on, the stones clicking, and you pour and pour, and say nothing. The fair one drinks every cup and smiles at you. The stern one drinks every cup and frowns at the board. You notice, after a long time, how strangely they sit: the fair one squarely, low and broad, not moving except to place a stone, the way a tortoise sits on a rock; the stern one coiled on himself, quick, his hand darting out to the board and back. At last the stern one looks up. "Whose wine have we been drinking?"

choices.text: Tell them everything: the monk, the nineteen

effects.log: The fair one opens a book of names on the rock beside the board and finds you. "Nineteen," he says sadly. "We took the wine," says the stern one. "A debt is a debt." They argue, short and sharp, about whether that counts. Then the fair one takes the brush, and the stern one, grumbling, holds the book open, and with one stroke the one becomes a nine. "Ninety-nine," says the fair one. "Go home," says the stern one, "and stop stealing wine."

choices.text: Beg them, on your knees

ok.log: You beg, and the stern one is unmoved, and the fair one is moved, and they quarrel over your head for so long that the sun goes down. In the end the stern one throws up his hands: "Fine. But I write it." He takes the brush and adds the stroke himself, quick and neat. Ninety-nine.

fail.log: You beg so badly, so tearfully, that the stern one covers his face and the fair one has to laugh. "Oh, give it the nine," the stern one says at last through his fingers, "before it cries on the board." Ninety-nine.

events.text: Your nineteenth year. In the spring a cart loses its wheel on the steep lane and comes down at you sideways, and there is nowhere to go. It stops a hand's breadth from your chest, against nothing, as if it had hit a wall of stone. People run up shouting. On the road where the cart stopped, pressed into the dust, is a print that might be the edge of a great shell, and a thin curving line beside it.

choices.text: Climb the mountain again with wine

effects.log: The rock under the pine is empty, the board gone. But there are two cups on the rock, clean and dry, as if set out for someone who was expected. You fill them both. When you come back at dusk they are empty, and the pine smells of deep water.

choices.text: Go to the river and bow to the north

effects.log: You do not know why the north. You only know it is right. You bow three times on the bank, and a long way off, under the water, something slow and something quick are, you are almost certain, very pleased with themselves.

events.text: You have taken work as ferry hand to the old woman who runs the crossing below the village, who has poled the same river for fifty years and swears at it like an old spouse. In the first flood of your first summer the river comes down roaring, and she pushes off anyway with a full boat. Halfway across the boat goes level and still in the middle of the torrent, as if set on a table. She does not look surprised. She reaches into her sleeve and throws a handful of millet over the side.

choices.text: Ask her what is under the boat

effects.log: "The old one," she says. "Under the ford. Two heads. One of them is rude." She spits in the river companionably. "Fifty years. Every flood. I pay it in millet. It does not need millet. It likes being paid."

choices.text: Throw a handful of your own millet after hers

effects.log: She watches you do it and grunts, which from her is a speech of welcome. "Good," she says. "Now it knows your hand."

choices.text: Grab the pole from her and steer

ok.log: You fight the pole and the boat does not care: it goes where it was going, level and slow. She laughs at you all the way to the far bank. "Strong arms," she says. "Useless. Let the river carry you, it is better at it."

fail.log: The pole kicks in the current and catches you in the ribs. You sit in the bottom of the boat the rest of the way while it crosses by itself. (-6 health)

events.text: The ferry woman is dying, in her hut by the landing, and asks you to row her out to the middle of the river one last time. Not across. Just out. In the middle of the current you ship the oars, and she leans over the side and talks to the water, low, for a long time, like somebody saying goodbye to an old neighbour across a fence.

choices.text: Keep the boat steady and look away

effects.log: You look at the far bank. Behind you she talks, and once laughs, and once the boat rocks as if something had put its chin on the side of it. When she says take me home, her face is wet and she looks twenty years younger. She dies that winter. At the burial the river freezes a day early, all at once, very smooth, like a laid cloth.

choices.text: Listen

effects.log: She is telling it about you: that you are lazy and strong and will do. That the millet is in the second jar. That she is sorry about the year she cursed it for drowning a calf, and it was not its fault. Under the water, two voices, faint as bubbles, answer her. You will never tell anyone what they said.

events.text: The ferry is yours now. The first flood of the first summer without her, you push off with a full boat into a brown roaring river, and halfway across nothing happens. The boat bucks. The passengers scream. You remember the second jar.

choices.text: Throw the millet over the side, and say her name

effects.log: A handful of millet and her name, shouted into the flood. The boat goes level as if set on a table. On the far bank an old farmer, white to the lips, asks what you said. "I paid the fare," you tell him. You pay it every flood after, for the rest of your working life.

choices.text: Pole for your life

ok.log: You get them across by main force and luck, and collapse on the bank. That night you take the millet jar down to the water and sit there for an hour, apologising. The next flood, the boat goes level.

fail.log: The boat goes over in the shallows on the far side. Everybody lives, which is a miracle, and on the bank you find a passenger's lost child sitting in the reeds perfectly dry, saying a big black stone carried it. (-15 health)

events.text: The carpenter you work for has a commission for a rich family's new gate, and gives you the bolt to carve, the long bar that slides across: a pair of turtles facing each other at the ends, for long life, the old way. You have carved turtles before. But tonight, working late by the lamp, you look up and there is a real one on the workshop threshold, black, with a black snake round its shell, watching you carve two turtles where it is one.

choices.text: Carve one turtle with a snake round it instead

ok.log: You carve it as you see it: one shell, the snake wound round, the two heads turned to face each other along the bolt. The carpenter scolds you for breaking with the pattern, and then stands looking at it for a long time. The family pays double. On the threshold, at dawn, there is a wet print of a shell, and the snake's thin line beside it, as if something had sat there approving until the work was done.

fail.log: The snake comes out looking like a belt and the tortoise like a bun. The carpenter takes the bolt away and carves the ordinary two turtles himself. But he keeps your failed one, you notice, on the shelf above his bench.

choices.text: Carve the two turtles as ordered

effects.log: Two turtles facing each other, as ordered. When you look up the threshold is empty. In the morning the turtle on the left end of the bolt has, somehow, a scratch round its shell like a thread wound round it. You did not make it. You leave it.

events.text: Years later you walk past the gate you carved for. The family has fallen on hard times, the gate is grey and the roof tiles slipping, and the last of the line lives there alone now. But the old woman sits on the step every evening with her hand on the gate bolt, and she is ninety-three.

choices.text: Ask her about the bolt

effects.log: "Long life," she says, patting the carved shell. "It works, you know. Too well. Everybody else is dead." She laughs, a dry quick laugh, and then, more slowly, sadly, as if she were two people. "But I would not trade it."

choices.text: Oil the bolt and mend the gate for her, for nothing

effects.log: A day's work. When you slide the bolt home at the end, it moves as sweetly as the day you made it. She makes you barley tea. You leave feeling that the carving has come round and blessed its carver.

events.text: Your sect elder sends you to the market town with a purse and an errand: a hundred-year shell for the hall's divination rite. Most shells in the curio shops are fifty-year shells with a hundred-year story. But {npc}, who keeps a shop of bones and roots behind the salt market, brings out from under the counter a whole black shell with thirteen great plates, cold as a stone from a well, and when you take it in your hands it is not empty. Something inside it says, in a small dry voice: "Put us down."

choices.text: Put it down very carefully

effects.log: You set it on the counter as if it were full of lamp oil. {npc} stares at you. "It never says anything to me," {npc} says, half offended. A thin black head comes out of the front of the shell and looks at you both, and goes back in.

choices.text: Buy it, quickly, before anybody else hears (20 taels)

effects.log: Twenty taels, every coin of the elder's purse and some of your own. {npc} wraps it in cloth without meeting your eye. All the way back to the hall it is heavy, and twice you hear, from inside the cloth, a slow voice and a quick one arguing in low tones about you.

choices.text: Ask {npc} where it came from

effects.log: "A northern river," {npc} says. "A fisherman found it asleep on a sandbank in the first frost and thought it was dead." A pause. "It was not." The shell, under your hands, gives a small offended shrug.

events.text: The shell from the curio shop is a living tortoise with a snake round it, and it has been asleep on a shelf in your room for a month, waking at night to argue. Tonight the snake puts its head out and speaks plainly. "Your elder means to heat us at the solstice and read the hall's future in our cracks. We can tell you the hall's future now, for nothing. It is a long one, if the shell is not cracked."

choices.text: Carry them north to a cold river before the solstice

effects.log: Twenty days north on foot with a heavy bundle, telling the elder you have gone home to a sick relative. At the river you unwrap them on the ice. The tortoise walks to the edge slowly; the snake looks back. "The hall will prosper," it says. "Not because of anything you did. We just thought you should know."

choices.text: Ask the snake to read your own future first

ok.log: "Only if you carry us north," the snake says. You do. On the ice of the river it reads you, quick and sure, and you will not repeat what it said to anybody, ever, except that it was mostly good and entirely true.

fail.log: "Only if you carry us north," it says, and you haggle, and the tortoise sighs a slow bubble of disgust. In the end you carry them north anyway, and on the ice the snake says only, "You haggle with the future. Stop that."

choices.text: Give it to the elder, as ordered

effects.log: You give it up. At the solstice the elder lights the brazier, lifts the shell, and finds it empty: a perfect shell, and nothing in it, and on the windowsill of your room a long shed snake skin, folded like a letter, addressed to nobody.

events.text: {npc} of the curio shop sends a boy for you. A northern fisherman has brought in another shell, black, huge, and {npc} wants your opinion before buying, being, {npc} says, the only person who has ever been spoken to by one.

choices.text: Go, and listen to it

effects.log: It is a shell, nothing more, old and empty and honourable. You tell {npc} so. {npc} buys it anyway and puts it in the window with a card: Not a talking one. It sells the next day for a great deal of money to someone who did not believe the card.

choices.text: Tell {npc} to stop buying shells

effects.log: {npc} grumbles. But the next time a fisherman comes in from the north with a black shell, the shop is selling dried roots and only dried roots, and the card in the window says: No shells. A friend asked.

events.text: Midwinter, and the county has called every strong back to the frozen river to cut ice for the royal ice house: great blocks sawn out and dragged by night on sledges, packed in straw, to keep the king cool all summer and the sick and the old a little cooler. Working a hole near the middle, you look down through ice as clear as glass, and far below, on the dark bed of the river, something is looking up: a shell as wide as a cart, and two heads.

choices.text: Move your hole away from it

effects.log: You drag your saw ten paces to the side without explaining. The foreman curses you. All night you work, and the ice you cut is the clearest on the river, and it does not melt on the sledge the way the others' does.

choices.text: Call the others to look

effects.log: By the time they come with torches, there is only dark water under clear ice. They laugh at you for a week. But the oldest cutter, at the end of the week, says quietly that his father saw the same thing in the winter of the great frost, and that the ice that year kept until autumn.

choices.text: Tap on the ice, three times

ok.log: Three taps. Far below, slowly, one head lifts toward you. Then the other, quickly. Two taps come back up through the ice, one slow, one quick. You do not tell anyone. You cut the rest of your blocks with the strange feeling of working under supervision.

fail.log: You tap, and lean too far, and your foot goes through a soft patch into water so cold it stops your breath. The others haul you out. Under the ice, nothing. (-5 health)

events.text: High summer and a fever in the town, the old and the small burning up, and the ice house's ration all gone to the palace and the officials. You know a thing nobody else does: under the clear ice in the middle of the river, last winter, there was a cold that did not come from the winter.

choices.text: Go down to the river at night and ask

effects.log: You kneel on the bank in the hot dark and ask, aloud, for the town. Nothing. Then, toward dawn, a mist comes off the river, cool as a cellar, and lies in the streets until noon, and the fevers break, one house at a time. The physician says it was the weather.

choices.text: Take what you can from the ice house by night

ok.log: You break the lock and carry out three blocks on your back, one at a time, to the street of the poorest houses. Nobody ever finds out who. Under the straw, the third block had something frozen in its heart: a thin black curl, like a shed snake skin. You leave it on the river bank.

fail.log: The ice house guard catches you with the first block and beats you. But he lets the block go to the sick street anyway, and stands looking at it melting in the dust for a long time. (-10 health)

events.text: A warm winter: the river does not freeze at all. No ice to cut, none for the ice house, and the elders say that means fever next summer and bodies that cannot be kept for their funerals. The magistrate has ordered a black ox and black millet offered at the ice house door to the god of cold, the old rite. You are one of those holding the ox.

choices.text: Pray with them, properly, facing north

effects.log: The rite is long and nobody really believes in it. You do, for the length of it. On the third night after, the river freezes in one night from bank to bank, with a sound like a great slow breath let out, and the ice cutters are out by dawn.

choices.text: Slip away to the river and wait on the bank

effects.log: You sit on the bank in the mild dark. Near midnight, far out on the water, two heads rise, close together, and look at the ice house on the hill and the torches of the rite. Then they sink, and the river begins, from the middle outward, to freeze.

events.text: A fortune-teller at the market heats turtle plastrons over a brazier for a copper and reads the cracks. Most of it is nonsense. But when your turn comes and the bone cracks in the heat, the fortune-teller stops talking, looks at the cracks for a long time, and then pushes the copper back across the table. "Not for this one," he says. "The shell says somebody else is reading you already. Somebody with two heads."

choices.text: Ask what that means

effects.log: "It means," he says, "that something old has taken an interest. Do not worry. The old ones are mostly patient." He thinks. "Mostly." You go home and for weeks you catch yourself watching wells.

choices.text: Ask him whose shell he is burning

effects.log: He goes red. "River turtles," he says. "Dead ones. Mostly." You leave. The next market day his stall is gone, and in its place a sign in an untidy hand: Gone fishing. Will read hands instead.

events.text: Years after the fortune-teller, on a cold night, you dream you are lying on your back on a rock in a river, and something is reading the lines on your palm with a quick dry tongue, and something else, slow, is writing down what the first one says.

choices.text: Ask the slow one what it wrote

effects.log: "Nothing yet," says a voice like a stone turning in deep water. "We only write endings. Yours is a long way off." You wake up comforted in a way you could not explain to anybody.

choices.text: Ask the quick one what it read

effects.log: "That you will cheat at baduk once and be caught," says a voice like dry leaves, "and that it will be the best evening of your life." It is right, years later, about both.

events.text: You grind ink for a painter who is making a screen of the ten long-lived things for a lord's sixtieth birthday: sun, cloud, mountain, water, rock, pine, crane, deer, the herb of long life, and the turtle. The turtle is giving the painter trouble. "It looks like a stone with legs," he says, "and a turtle should look like a thousand years." That night you dream of a black shell and a snake, and wake knowing how it should look.

choices.text: Tell the painter about your dream

effects.log: He listens, sceptical, and then paints a black shell with a snake wound round it, the heads turned toward each other, in the water below the pine. "It looks like a thousand years," he admits, "and an argument." The lord loves it. The screen stands in the hall for generations.

choices.text: Paint it yourself, while he sleeps

ok.log: You paint it by lamplight, the tortoise and its snake, slow and quick. In the morning the painter stands looking at it for a long time, then signs the screen and adds your name beside his in small characters. He has never done that for anyone.

fail.log: The snake comes out looking like a worm in a hurry. The painter scrapes it off without a word and paints the stone with legs. But that night he dreams of a black shell and a snake too, and in the morning he paints it again, and it is right.

events.text: Long after, in a great house you are visiting, you find the screen of the ten long-lived things, its silk browned with age. The sun has faded and the deer has lost an ear to a careless servant. But the black tortoise and its snake in the water under the pine are as dark and fresh as wet ink, as if somebody came in every night to look after them.

choices.text: Touch the shell on the silk

effects.log: The silk is cold under your finger, colder than the room, the way the river is cold in the north. The old steward of the house says nobody touches that panel. Nobody needs to. It keeps itself.

choices.text: Ask the household about it

effects.log: Every head of the house for generations, the steward says, has lived past eighty. They give the credit to the pine. You do not correct them. The pine has been very decent about it.

events.text: A medicine house in the capital has hired you to guard its turtle catchers for a season on the northern rivers: nine rough men with nets and reed traps who take every shell they can find, alive, for the brazier men and the bone-grinders. The pay is good. On the third morning the catchers come running back up the bank, white-faced, without their nets. Something in the reeds, they say, bit through every net at once, and then spoke to them.

choices.text: Go down into the reeds alone and see

ok.log: In the reeds, waist-deep in cold water, a black shell as wide as a cart, and a snake with its head raised, looking straight at you. "Go home," it says, in a reasonable voice. "Or catch frogs. The frogs will not mind." The tortoise says nothing. It simply waits, the way a cliff waits for a ship. You go back up the bank and tell the catchers the season is over.

fail.log: You wade into the reeds with your sword out, and something takes your legs out from under you like a log rolling, and you go under. When you come up, coughing, your sword is lying on the bank, neatly, hilt toward you. (-10 health)

choices.text: Tell the catchers it is a sign, and take them home

effects.log: You call it a sign, loudly, in front of the oldest catcher, who is relieved to agree. The medicine house docks your pay. You do not mind. On the last night, camped on the bank, you wake to find the cage on the cart open and empty and the water outside it full of small heads going home.

choices.text: Drive them back into the river: you are paid by the shell

effects.log: You drive them back in with the flat of your sword. They catch eleven brown turtles that day and lose two men to a sudden current that came from nowhere. You are paid by the shell. You do not sleep well on the way home.

events.text: The medicine house asks you to guard its catchers again, for twice the pay: the black tortoise of the northern reeds is worth more than all the rest together, they say, and they want it this year. The oldest catcher comes to see you the night before you leave, alone, holding his hat.

choices.text: Refuse the job, and tell him why

effects.log: He listens and nods. "My grandfather caught turtles," he says. "He said there was one you must never take. Two heads. It writes things down." He puts on his hat. "I am going to sell fish instead." He does, and grows quite fat on it.

choices.text: Take the job, and lead them to the wrong river

ok.log: A month on a muddy southern river where nothing lives but eels. The medicine house is furious and pays you half. On the road home a snow goose follows you for three days, which in the north, the old catcher says, is somebody saying thank you.

fail.log: The catchers see through you in a week and go north without you. They find nothing: the reeds are empty, the water still. But the house blames you anyway, and you never work for it again.

events.text: You came north as the sworn guard of an envoy from the south, and the northern king has thrown you both into a prison yard with a stone well in the middle of it, and says the envoy may go home when the south gives back two provinces it never had. The envoy cannot give them. Every night you sit by the well, because it is the only place in the yard the guards cannot see. Every night, from far down the well, you hear two voices arguing very quietly.

choices.text: Lean over the well and listen

effects.log: One voice slow, one quick. They are arguing about a rabbit. The slow one says the rabbit was a liar; the quick one says the rabbit was a genius. They go on for an hour. You fall asleep on the cold stone smiling for the first time in a month.

choices.text: Drop a pebble down the well

effects.log: It goes down a long way and does not splash. Both voices stop. After a while, very small, the quick one says: "Rude." The slow one says nothing at all, which is somehow worse. You do not drop another.

events.text: A courtier of the northern court visits the prison yard at night with a jar of wine and a bribe in his sleeve, and sits by the well with the envoy and with you, and tells, as if idly, an old story. The Dragon King of the sea was sick and could be cured only by a rabbit's liver. A turtle went ashore and lured a rabbit down to the palace. And the rabbit, when it understood, said: what a pity, I left my liver on the mountain to dry. The courtier drinks, and leaves. The envoy sits very still. From the bottom of the well, a quick dry voice whispers: "And the turtle took the rabbit back to the shore to fetch it."

choices.text: Tell the envoy what the well said

effects.log: The envoy understands at once. In the morning the envoy writes to the northern king: of course the provinces will be returned, gladly, only the envoy must first go home to persuade the south. The northern king reads it twice, and laughs, and believes it.

choices.text: Ask the well what happened to the turtle afterwards

effects.log: "It went home," says the slow voice, "and told the truth to the Dragon King. And was not punished. And was very embarrassed for three hundred years." The envoy, listening beside you, has understood the story perfectly and is already writing a letter.

events.text: The northern king has let you go, with an escort, to the border river. On the far bank is the south. In the middle of the ford the envoy turns in the saddle and calls back to the escort, clearly and cheerfully: tell your king the rabbit thanks him, and its liver is quite safe. The escort's captain draws his sword.

choices.text: Hold the ford while the envoy crosses

ok.log: You turn your horse in the water and hold the escort at the ford until the envoy is across. Then the river does something odd: it rises, slow and broad, under the escort's horses, as if something enormous had stood up on the riverbed. They go back. You ride across on water that is suddenly only knee-deep.

fail.log: The captain's blade opens your arm, and you are falling, and then you are not: something under the water has lifted you and your horse together and is carrying you across, slowly, broad and steady, while arrows hiss into the river behind. (-18 health)

choices.text: Laugh, and spur across beside the envoy

effects.log: You both spur across laughing like children. The escort's arrows fall short every one, as if the air over the ford were thicker than air should be. On the far bank, looking back, you see two heads lift out of the middle of the river, watch you go, and sink.

events.text: The envoy you guarded in the north became king, reigned well, and has died, old. The new king, the son, has sent men all over the kingdom to find the finest turtle in the land to carry his father's stele: a stone turtle, carved from life. They have come to you, because you were there, and they want to know: was there a turtle in that well?

choices.text: Tell them, and send them north to the right river

effects.log: You tell them about the well, the two voices, the rabbit. They go north. You hear, a year later, that the carvers came back with sketches of a tortoise that would not sit still, that strode about the riverbank with its head lifted as if it were glad to see them, and that the stele turtle they made is the most cheerful stone in the kingdom.

choices.text: Tell them it was only a well

effects.log: They carve an ordinary turtle, solemn and heavy. It is a good stele. But you go north alone in the spring, to the river, and tell the water that the rabbit's king is dead, and that he never forgot. Under the ice, something slow listens all the way to the end.

events.text: Your old teacher is failing, and will not say how long there is. On a cold river in the north, where your teacher once took you as a child, there is said to be a turtle with a snake round it that reads endings. You go alone and sit on the bank until, at dusk, a thin black head rises out of the water. "Ask," it says.

choices.text: Ask the snake when your teacher will die

effects.log: "The first day of the first snow," the snake says, "two winters from now." It looks at you. "You wanted to know. Now you know. It is heavier than not knowing." Beside it the tortoise lifts its head, very slowly, and says in a voice like a stone settling: "We will be there."

choices.text: Ask the tortoise instead to be there when it happens

effects.log: The snake looks offended to be passed over. The tortoise lifts its head out of the water, slowly, and looks at you for a long time. "Yes," it says. One word, like a stone set down. The snake mutters: "Two winters. The first snow. Since nobody asked."

choices.text: Ask nothing, and go home

effects.log: You stand up without asking and go home. Behind you the snake says, "Wise," and sounds disappointed. Your teacher dies when your teacher dies, and you are there, and it is enough.

events.text: Two winters on, the first snow. Your teacher has asked to be carried to the river, and lies on a pallet on the bank wrapped in quilts, watching the flakes fall on the black water. On a rock in the middle of the river, as still as the rock, there is a shell, and a thin black head raised beside it.

choices.text: Tell your teacher what is on the rock

effects.log: Your teacher laughs, very weakly. "Witnesses," your teacher says. "Good. Somebody should write it down properly. You would only make it beautiful." Your teacher dies before dark, laughing. On the rock the tortoise lowers its head once, the way a scribe lowers a brush, and the river freezes over in a single breath.

choices.text: Say nothing, and hold your teacher's hand

effects.log: You hold the cold hand until it is colder. When you look up, the rock is empty and the river is freezing, slowly, from the middle outward, smooth as a shroud. Downstream, something is going north with a new plate on its back, written true.

events.text: Long after your teacher's death a snow goose lands at your door with a scrap of black shell in its beak, hexagonal, thin as paper. On it, small and square and very plain, is written your teacher's last day: the snow, the pallet, the laugh. Nothing is beautiful about it. Every word is true.

choices.text: Keep it in your teacher's spirit tablet shrine

effects.log: It sits beside the tablet. On the anniversary each year the scrap is cold to the touch and the room smells of river. You find you grieve better for having it: plainly, without decoration, the way your teacher would have wanted.

choices.text: Write your own account beside it

effects.log: You write it beautifully, of course. You put the two side by side. The beautiful one is yours. The true one is the river's. Your teacher, you think, would have laughed at both, and kept both.

events.text: You ride with a young archer of the north and his three companions, fleeing his brothers, who mean to kill him. Behind you on the plain, torches: the horsemen. In front of you, a wide black river with no bridge and no boat. The archer reins in at the water's edge, strikes the river with his bow, and shouts across it that he is the son of heaven and the grandson of the river, and will the river let him drown?
events.arc: The Bridge of Fish and Turtles

choices.text: Ride into the water beside him

ok.log: The river rises under your horse's hooves: backs. Fish, a thousand, ten thousand, and turtles among them, shell to shell, a road of living backs across the black water. Your horse steps on a broad black shell in the middle, with a snake wound round it, and the snake looks up at you as you pass and says, "Do not stop." You do not stop.

fail.log: Your horse balks at the edge and you go in on foot, and the water is up to your chest, and then something broad and cold comes up under your feet and carries you, and you cross on it soaked and gasping behind the others. (-10 health)

choices.text: Turn and hold the riverbank so he can cross

ok.log: You turn alone against the torches. By the time the first riders reach you, the archer is across, and behind you the river is a road of backs, and you back your horse onto it, still fighting, and the backs carry you across too. Then they sink, and the riders on the near bank sit their horses at the water's edge and cannot follow.

fail.deathCause: the horsemen at the river with no bridge
fail.log: You hold the bank long enough. That was the point.

choices.text: Say it is madness and look for a ford

effects.log: You ride off along the bank looking for a ford. Behind you, a sound like the whole river taking a breath. When you look back, the archer and his companions are on the far bank and the river is sinking back to black, and you are on the wrong side of it, alone, with torches coming.

events.text: The archer you crossed the river with has founded a kingdom on the far side, and built a hall, and made you a lord of it. At the first great feast the new king stands and pours a cup of wine into the river, and orders that no fisher of the kingdom shall ever net a turtle in that water.
events.arc: The Bridge of Fish and Turtles

choices.text: Raise a cup to the bridge

effects.log: You raise your cup of tea. The whole hall raises theirs. A long way down the river, something slow and something quick feel, you are sure, a very great number of people raising cups to them at once, and are embarrassed, and pleased.

choices.text: Ask the king to also forbid the shell braziers

ok.log: The king thinks about it, and then agrees, and the court diviners grumble, and from that year no living shell is heated anywhere in the kingdom. It is the best law you will ever have a hand in.

fail.log: The court diviners talk the king out of it. You lose that argument. But the king, at the end of the feast, quietly gives you his own diviner's brazier to melt down, and you make a bell of it.

events.text: A hard year in the south: no rain, no king worth the name, and the elders of nine villages have decided to do the oldest thing they know. They climb the turtle-headed hill at dawn, the one shaped like a turtle putting its head out of its shell, and stamp the earth, and sing the old song at it: Turtle, turtle, put forth your head. If you do not, we will roast you and eat you. You have been hired to guard them. Under your feet, as they sing, the hill moves. Very slightly. Like something waking.

choices.text: Sing with them

effects.log: You join in, loud and badly. Under your feet the hill shivers again, twice: once slow and once quick, as if two heads had heard the song and were arguing about which one it was meant for. The rain comes that evening. The elders say it was the song. You think it was the argument.

choices.text: Kneel and put your hand on the ground

ok.log: Under your palm the earth is cold, and very far down, something is breathing, slow, and something else is listening, quick. You understand, without words, that the hill is not the turtle, only its shape; the turtle is somewhere north, and has heard, and is deciding.

fail.log: You feel nothing but stones and the sweat of your own palm. But when you stand up, every one of the nine elders is staring at you, because there is a damp print on the ground where your hand was, shaped like a shell.

choices.text: Keep watch on the road: guarding is the job

effects.log: You watch the road. Nobody comes. The elders sing until noon, and come down hoarse and happy. The rain comes three days later. You were paid to guard, and you guarded, and you are left with the uneasy sense of having missed the only part that mattered.

events.text: Years after the singing on the turtle-headed hill, a child is found in the hollow at its crown at dawn, alone, wrapped in red cloth, nobody's. The nine villages argue over who should raise it. They have asked you to judge, as the one who stood on the hill the morning it moved.

choices.text: Give the child to all nine villages together

effects.log: Nine households take turns, a year each. The child grows up belonging to everybody and quarrelling with nobody. Long after, you hear that the nine villages have made the grown child their headman, and that the child insists on a song at every harvest: turtle, turtle, put forth your head.

choices.text: Ask the hill

ok.log: You climb to the crown alone at dusk and ask. The ground shivers, twice, slow and then quick. You go down and say: the village that fed the singers on the hill that morning. It was the poorest of the nine. They raise the child well.

fail.log: The hill says nothing. You decide by drawing straws, which nobody likes. But the child, when it can talk, walks across all nine villages alone in one day, and sits down at the poorest gate, and stays.

events.text: War on a river: two armies on two banks, and every boat burned. On the north bank a herdsman soldier has been given leave to die tomorrow in the first charge, and has written a letter to the weaver who waits for him on the south bank, where the enemy is. He asks you, because you are strong enough to try, to carry it over tonight. It is the seventh night of the seventh month, when the herd boy and the weaver girl of the sky meet on a bridge of magpies.

choices.text: Swim it across at midnight

ok.log: Halfway, in the black middle of the river, your strength goes. Then there is something broad and cold under your chest, carrying you, slow and level, and a voice by your ear, quick and dry: "Keep the letter out of the water. Ink runs." You reach the south bank with the letter dry above your head.

fail.log: The current takes you a mile downstream and you nearly drown, and come ashore with the letter soaked in your fist. But when you open it on the bank, the ink has not run at all, not one stroke, as if something had held it above the water the whole way. (-14 health)

choices.text: Ask the river to carry it

effects.log: You fold the letter into a cup of oiled paper, set it on the water, and ask aloud, feeling foolish. The cup does not drift. It goes straight across, against the current, as if something under it were swimming. On the far bank, a lantern lifts.

events.text: On the south bank the weaver reads the letter by lantern, and does not cry, and writes an answer on the back of it, and asks you to take it back across before dawn, before the charge. Beside the lantern, half out of the water at the landing, a black shell is waiting, as broad as a doorstep. The snake round it looks at the letter, and then at you. "Read it," it says. "I did. You should know what you are carrying."

choices.text: Carry it back without reading it

effects.log: You fold it into your collar and step onto the shell. It carries you over in the dark, slow and level. On the north bank the herdsman reads it in the grey light and laughs out loud, and that morning the charge is called off: a truce, from nowhere. You never learn what the weaver wrote. The tortoise, you suspect, wrote it down.

choices.text: Read it, as the snake says

effects.log: It says only: Do not die tomorrow. I have finished the cloth. It says nothing about war, which is somehow the most important thing about it. You carry it back over on the black shell, and the herdsman reads it, and goes to his captain, and talks for a long time, and the charge is not made.

choices.text: Let the snake improve it a little

effects.log: "She should mention the stars," says the snake, and adds a line in a quick slanting hand. The tortoise shakes its head, slowly, and carries you over anyway. The herdsman reads it and weeps at the line about the stars, which was not hers. You feel, for years, that you owe the weaver an apology.

events.text: The war on the river is long over. On the seventh night of the seventh month you are invited to a wedding in a village on the south bank: an old herdsman and an old weaver, who have waited out a war and their parents and a great deal else. The bride wears a cloth she wove herself, and at the wedding table there is one place set at the end with nobody in it, and a bowl of river water.

choices.text: Ask who the empty place is for

effects.log: "For the one who carried the letters," the bride says, "and you, and the other one." She looks at the bowl of water. "The one with two heads." When the wedding feast is over, the bowl is empty, and on the table beside it is a wet print of a shell.

choices.text: Give a toast to the river

effects.log: You stand up and give a toast to the river, which nobody understands but the bride and the groom and you. Magpies wheel over the village all evening, though it is dark. Far off, in the river, two heads come up to look at the lanterns.

events.text: {npc}, the alchemist of your sect, has a theory: the Black Tortoise Iron Canon, the northern qi method that hardens the body like a shell, was first read in the grain of a living shell, and copies of copies have lost half of it. {npc} has caught a black tortoise in the north, with a snake round it, and keeps it in a cold cellar. Your task is to sit with it by lamplight and read the grain of its plates, line by line, and copy what you find.
events.arc: The Iron Canon in the Shell

choices.text: Read the grain, carefully, and copy only what is there

ok.log: It is slow work. The grain moves when you are not looking, and the snake watches your brush. But it is there: the lost half of the Canon, breath by breath, the way the north water hardens and does not break. On the last night the tortoise lifts its head and looks at your copy, and blinks, once, slowly. You think it approves.

fail.log: You copy what you think is there, and the snake leans over and says, "That is a scratch from an otter, in the year of the long flood." You start again. It takes a year. You learn more about otters than about qi.

choices.text: Ask the snake to read it to you

effects.log: "Ah," the snake says, delighted to be asked. "Of course." It reads you the Canon in a quick dry voice, and you copy it, and only later, practising it, do you find that the snake has improved several lines. They work. They work better, in fact. The tortoise sighs a long slow bubble in the corner.

choices.text: Tell {npc} you will not read a living shell

effects.log: {npc} stares, then shrugs and sends another disciple. That night you go down to the cellar and unbar the door and leave it open. In the morning the cellar is empty, and {npc} says nothing about it to anyone, ever, and looks at you very differently afterwards.

events.text: {npc} has read your copy of the Canon and wants the rest, the part your copy says is written on the inside of the shell, where no lamp can reach. The furnace is lit. {npc} means to take the shell off the tortoise to read it, and says, reasonably, that a thousand disciples will be stronger for it.
events.arc: The Iron Canon in the Shell

choices.text: Stand between {npc} and the cellar door

ok.log: It is a fight in the corridor of the alchemy hall with the furnace roaring behind you. You win it. {npc} sits on the floor among broken jars and laughs, bitterly, and then not bitterly.
