"The inside of the shell," {npc} says. "Of course it was never meant to be read." The cellar is opened that night.

fail.deathCause: the alchemist's furnace, between a door and a living shell
fail.log: You held the door long enough for the snake to bite through the bars.

choices.text: Tell {npc} the inside of the shell is blank

ok.log: "I asked," you lie. "The snake told me. Blank. Only endings get written there." {npc} looks at you a long time and lets the furnace go out. The next morning the cellar door is found open. {npc} does not chase it.

fail.log: {npc} does not believe you and goes down to the cellar with a knife. The cellar is empty. The bars are bitten through. {npc} blames you, rightly, and you are confined to your quarters for a year. (-8 health)

choices.text: Go down to the cellar and ask the tortoise what to do

effects.log: The tortoise looks at you for a long time. Then the snake says, "It says: open the door. It says the inside of a shell is the inside of a life. It says thank you for asking." You open the door. You lose your place in the sect. You do not, in the end, mind.

events.text: You are a captain of the palace guard in the last years of an old kingdom. At midnight a ghost runs through the palace halls crying that the kingdom will fall, and sinks into the earth of the inner garden. The king orders the spot dug up. Three feet down the diggers find a turtle, alive, black, with a snake round its shell, and on its back, in characters as fresh as wet ink: This kingdom is a full moon. The kingdom across the river is a new moon.

choices.text: Fetch the court shaman to read it

effects.log: The shaman reads it and goes grey. "A full moon wanes," the shaman says. "A new moon waxes." The king has the shaman taken away. Behind you, in the pit, very quietly, the snake says to the tortoise: "I did not write it." The tortoise says, slowly: "I know. I saw who did."

choices.text: Cover the pit and say nothing to the king

effects.log: You order the earth put back. The diggers look at you. In the morning the pit is open again, from the inside, and empty, and the king hears anyway from a gardener. The shaman is sent for. You did not stop anything. You only made it later.

events.text: The shaman who read the turtle's back is in prison and will be executed at dawn for saying that the kingdom will fall. You have the keys to that prison. The kingdom will fall: you have seen the army across the river, and the empty granaries, and the king.

choices.text: Let the shaman out before dawn

effects.log: You open the door and walk the shaman to the river gate yourself. At the gate the shaman takes your hand. "It wrote it," the shaman says. "Not the turtle. The ghost. I saw the ink on its fingers." Then the shaman is gone into the dark, and you go back to your post and wait for whatever comes.

choices.text: Go to the king and argue for the shaman's life

ok.log: You argue all night. In the end the king, very tired, commutes it to exile. "A full moon," the king says to you at dawn, alone, "is still full tonight." You think it is the wisest thing you have heard that king say.

fail.log: The king has you beaten from the hall. The shaman dies at dawn. But that night, in the garden, you find the pit dug open again and, in the earth at the bottom, a print of a shell and, beside it, a thin line of characters too small to read. (-8 health)

choices.text: Do your duty

effects.log: You keep the keys on your belt. At dawn it is done. That summer the kingdom across the river comes over it, as the shell said, and the palace burns, and somewhere in the smoke a turtle is walking slowly north, carrying it all on its back.

events.text: The old kingdom fell that summer, as the shell said. Years later, a refugee in another country, you see in a market a scribe selling copies of the turtle's oracle as a lucky charm: a full moon and a new moon, drawn badly. The scribe has added a tortoise underneath, with a snake round it, and the snake is winking.

choices.text: Buy one, for old times

effects.log: One copper. You pin it inside your door. It is the only thing you own from the old kingdom, and it is a joke, and you find you like it better than any treasure you might have saved.

choices.text: Tell the scribe the true story

effects.log: The scribe listens to all of it: the ghost, the pit, the shaman, the snake that said it did not write it. Then the scribe draws a new charm: the tortoise with its head lifted, looking straight out of the paper, saying nothing. It sells much worse. You buy that one.

events.text: The court has made you overseer of a great dyke on the northern river: ten thousand corvee labourers, a season to build it, and your name on the stone at the end. At dusk, walking the new embankment, you look down and see a black shell in the shallows below, and a thin black head raised beside it. "It will fail," the snake says, matter of fact. "The third spring. At the bend. The earth there is sand under clay."

choices.text: Rebuild the bend, whatever it costs

ok.log: You tear out the bend and dig to the sand and pile stone, and the court fines you for the delay and the labourers curse you for the extra month. In the third spring the river comes down higher than anyone living has seen it, and the bend holds. In the shallows below it, a slow head comes up and looks at the stone for a long time, and sinks, as if something had decided there would be nothing to write.

fail.log: You rebuild the bend, but not deep enough: you cannot find the sand. In the third spring the bend leaks and does not break. Three fields are lost instead of three villages. On the bank, at dawn, you see the snake look at the tortoise, and the tortoise look at the snake, as if neither of them knew what to write.

choices.text: Ask the snake why it is telling you

effects.log: "Because the tortoise wants to watch it fail," the snake says, "and write it down. And I want to see if you can stop it. We have a wager." The tortoise says nothing. You go back up the embankment knowing you are the stakes.

choices.text: Finish on time and take your name on the stone

effects.log: You finish on time. Your name is cut into the stone. The court is pleased. The snake, when you walk the embankment the last night, is gone, but the tortoise is still there in the shallows below the bend, waiting, the way a scribe waits with the brush already wet.

events.text: The third spring. The river is coming down high and brown, and you ride to the bend of your dyke in the rain. In the shallows below, the black shell is waiting, as it said it would.

choices.text: Bring every labourer you can find and shore the bend

ok.log: Three days and nights in the rain with sandbags and logs and every pair of hands in the district. The bend shudders and holds. On the fourth morning the river drops. Below the bend, the tortoise lifts its head and looks at you, and you swear the snake beside it is grinning.

fail.log: The bend goes in the night, with a sound like a door slammed in heaven. You get the village out in time, every soul, but the fields are gone. At dawn the tortoise is on the broken bank with its head lowered over the water, and its plate, you feel, is being written. (-15 health)

choices.text: Ride to the villages below and get everyone out

effects.log: You do not try to save the dyke. You save the people. The bend breaks at midnight and the river takes the fields and the empty houses. Nobody dies. At dawn, on the broken bank, the tortoise lowers its head over the water, slowly, like a scribe signing. It is, you think, the best ending you could have given it to write.

events.text: On a journey along the eastern sea, your party stops for a midday meal on the rocks, and a great wave takes the magistrate's lady out of your midst as if a hand had reached up for her. An old man of the coast runs up shouting the old remedy: get everyone on the shore, strike the ground with sticks, and sing the turtle song, give back the lady, turtle, give her back, or we will net you and roast you. Many mouths, he says, can melt iron.

choices.text: Grab a stick and sing louder than anyone

effects.log: The whole coast sings, beating the rocks, and you loudest. Far out, the sea heaves. The lady walks out of the foam onto the rocks, dry, smelling of strange incense, and says the palace under the sea was very beautiful and the food was very good. Everyone looks at you, because you are hoarse. Somewhere in a cold northern river, you will learn much later, a turtle who had nothing to do with it heard the song and felt, all the same, a great urge to give something back.

choices.text: Dive in after her

ok.log: You go into the sea after her, and under the water there is a light and a gate of coral, and a turtle in a black gauze hat who looks at you with immense weariness and says, "Oh, very well," and pushes the lady back up toward the sun. You come up beside her, half drowned. The singing on the shore is very loud.

fail.deathCause: the eastern sea, diving after a lady the sea had taken
fail.log: The sea does not give back two.

events.text: Long after the day on the eastern rocks, you are standing by a cold river in the north when a black tortoise with a snake round its shell surfaces beside you, uninvited, and the snake says, in a voice like dry leaves: "Was it you? Singing on the eastern shore? It went all the way up the rivers. We had to give back a fish we were very fond of."

choices.text: Apologise, gravely

effects.log: The snake accepts the apology gravely. The tortoise, slowly, makes a sound in its throat that you realise, after a while, is a laugh. It is the first time you have heard a tortoise laugh. You will treasure it.

choices.text: Sing it again, softly, to see what happens

effects.log: You sing it, softly. The snake puts its head out further, against its will, and glares. The tortoise puts out its head too, slowly, from courtesy. "Many mouths melt iron," the snake says. "One mouth is just rude." But it does not go under until you have finished.

events.text: You command an army of the north under black flags, the colour of the north and of its guardian. Across the river a city is starving under siege by raiders, and will fall in three days. You can be there in one, if the river freezes by dawn. It is the first week of winter and the river is open, black and fast. Your scouts say that on a rock in the middle of it, every night this week, there has been a black shell, and something round it, watching your camp.

choices.text: Walk down to the bank alone and ask

effects.log: You stand at the water's edge and say it plainly: the city, the raiders, the dawn. On the rock, the snake turns to the tortoise. You hear it, very faintly, over the water: "Who pays?" A long silence. Then the tortoise lowers its head into the river, and the cold comes off it like breath.

choices.text: Order the army to cut rafts and cross the hard way

ok.log: A night of axes and rope. At dawn the first rafts go over in the black current, and the second, and by noon you are across with half your army and soaked to the bone. You raise the siege at dusk. On the rock in the middle of the river, as you pass, a slow head turns to watch you go, and you could swear it is impressed.

fail.log: Rafts go over. Men drown. You are across by the second dusk, too late for some of the city and in time for the rest. On the rock, something lowers its head over the water, slowly, the way a scribe lowers a brush. (-12 health)

choices.text: Ask the villages downstream first

effects.log: You ride to the fishing villages below the ford in the dark. If the river freezes three weeks early, their winter catch is lost. You ask them anyway. They argue for an hour and then the oldest fisher says: "Freeze it. We have relatives in that city." When you come back to the bank, the shell on the rock has turned to face the villages, as if it had been listening too.

events.text: Dawn. The river is white from bank to bank, a sheet of ice thick enough for horses, smooth as a laid floor, and steaming faintly with cold. In the middle, where the rock was, there is only ice, and under the ice, dark and broad, a shape.

choices.text: Lead the army across on foot, quietly

effects.log: Ten thousand men walk across in silence, because you have ordered silence, and every one of them looks down once, in the middle, at the dark shape under the ice, and walks on faster. You raise the siege by noon. That night the river breaks up again, all at once, three weeks too early for winter, as if something had let out a breath it was holding.

choices.text: Kneel on the ice first and thank it

effects.log: You kneel on the ice before your whole army, in your black armour, and bow to the shape beneath. Your soldiers think you have gone mad, and then, one by one, they kneel too. Under the ice the shape stirs. You cross. The siege is raised. For the rest of your life your army calls the river by a new name, which means The One Who Paid.

events.text: The fishing villages below the ford had a hard winter after the early freeze. You go back the next autumn with grain, and find them well enough, and find also that on the riverbank they have set up a small shrine of stones with a black flag on it, and in front of it, every morning, the children put a handful of millet.

choices.text: Leave the grain at the shrine too

effects.log: You leave the grain at the shrine, and the villagers share it, and the millet goes into the river as always. That winter the river freezes exactly on time, neither early nor late, and the fishing is the best in a few years.

choices.text: Ask who pays, as the snake asked

effects.log: "We did," the oldest fisher says. "A little. And it did, we think. It was very cold that night." She looks at the river. "And you. You came back." You find that the debt is settled, and that nobody owes anybody, and that this is a rarer thing than you thought.

events.text: War is coming over the sea, and the admiral of the southern coast has asked you, as a master of the arts of strength and form, to help the shipwrights with a new ship: covered, so no enemy can board it, low and broad and impossible to sink. For a week you draw and nothing is right. On the eighth morning there is a black tortoise as big as a threshing floor lying on the wet sand outside the shipyard door, with a snake round its shell, as if it had come to sit for its portrait.

choices.text: Draw it, exactly as it is

ok.log: You draw it all day: the broad back, the plates, the way the shell meets the water so that nothing can get a grip. At dusk the snake leans over your drawing and taps the back of it with its nose. "Spikes," it says. "On the roof. Then nobody will try to jump on it." You draw spikes. The admiral, seeing the drawing, says nothing for a long time, and then orders three.

fail.log: Your drawing is a turtle and not a ship. The tortoise looks at it with deep patience and does not move for three days, and on the third you understand: it is not a ship that floats like a turtle, it is a turtle that fights like a ship. You start again.

choices.text: Ask the snake what it would add

effects.log: "A head," the snake says at once. "At the front. That breathes smoke. So they cannot see what is coming." The tortoise looks at it. "Our head does not breathe smoke." "It could," the snake says. You draw a turtle's head at the bow with a chimney in its throat.

events.text: The covered ships go out against the enemy fleet at dawn, three of them, low and black with spikes on their roofs. Sulphur and saltpetre burn in the turtle heads at their bows, and a smoke like sea fog pours out ahead of them. From the admiral's flagship you watch the enemy try to board the first one and find nowhere to stand.

choices.text: Go aboard the lead ship yourself

ok.log: Inside the turtle it is dark and loud and smells of sulphur and oars. You fight at the gun ports all morning. When the smoke clears the enemy fleet is breaking, and under the keel of your ship, you would swear to it, something broad and black has been swimming the whole time, keeping it level.

fail.deathCause: a sea battle inside the covered ship you helped to draw
fail.log: It was the right shape. You were in the wrong place in it.

choices.text: Stay with the admiral and watch the line

effects.log: From the flagship you watch the turtle ships turn in the smoke like great slow beasts and break the enemy line. Far off in the bay, on a rock nobody else is looking at, a black shell with a snake round it is watching too, both heads up, very still.

events.text: Years after the war a young scholar comes to interview you for a history of the covered ships. He has a fine drawing of the bow from the records. "The dragon's head," he says, pointing. "Breathing smoke. A wonderful symbol."

choices.text: Correct him: it was a turtle's head

effects.log: He argues. Dragons are grander. You show him your own drawings, the tortoise on the sand, the snake's spikes. He goes away unconvinced, and writes dragon. Somewhere in the north, you imagine, a tortoise reads it and says nothing, and a snake says a great deal.

choices.text: Let him have his dragon

effects.log: You let it go. Histories are for the living. That night you dream of a broad black back under a keel in the smoke, and wake laughing, and do not know why.

events.text: Three auditors of heaven come down on a northern river in pale jade robes with ledgers under their arms. A creature of this river, they say, has been writing endings on its own back without a licence, and some of the endings are cracked, and heaven does not permit cracked records. They mean to take the shell up to be examined. You live by this river. You are strong enough to be in the way.

choices.text: Stand in their way and demand their warrant

ok.log: Their warrant is in order. Your fists are better. After a short, very formal fight on the ice the senior auditor straightens a crooked hat and writes, carefully: Inspection deferred. Local resistance. Under the ice, something slow and something quick are, you suspect, laughing.

fail.deathCause: three auditors of heaven on a northern river
fail.log: Their warrant was in order, and so were they.

choices.text: Ask to read the cracked plates yourself, as a witness

effects.log: The auditors confer and allow it. Under the ice the tortoise lifts its back to the surface, and you read: one crack, one ending the snake wrote without seeing. You testify that the rest are true. The auditors write: One crack. Mending recommended. They go. The snake, after, says to you: "Thank you for not lying for us."

choices.text: Invite them to tea and talk about something else

effects.log: Three days of tea, poetry and baduk. The auditors are, it turns out, very bored people who never get asked anything. They leave with full stomachs and an empty ledger page, and a promise to come back for a game next century.

events.text: A snow goose finds you with a scrap of black shell. On it, in a slow square hand: The crack is mended. We went back to the place and found the truth. It took a great many years. And under it, in a quick slanting hand: Tell the auditors. Gloat a little.

choices.text: Send the scrap up to heaven with your seal on it

effects.log: You send it. A month later a jade tablet comes down, very formal, closing the file. On the back, in tiny characters, someone has written: Next century. Baduk. You hang the tablet over your door.

choices.text: Keep it, and say nothing to anyone

effects.log: You keep it. Some records are better for being kept quietly. On the coldest night of each winter it hums faintly, like a stone that remembers being a shell.

events.text: You have beaten every master under heaven and there is only one name left on your list: the Black Warrior of the north, the tortoise with the snake round it. You find it on a frozen river and call it out to fight. The snake lifts its head. The tortoise lifts its head. They look at each other, and then both at you, and say together, perfectly reasonably: "Which of us?"

choices.text: The tortoise

ok.log: You fight the tortoise. It does nothing. For a day and a night you strike a shell that does not move, until your hands bleed and your qi runs dry, and at dawn you sit down in the snow, and the tortoise puts out its head and says: "Good." You have learned more about patience in one night than in a few years.

fail.log: You strike the shell until your wrist cracks. The tortoise does not move once. At dawn the snake says, "It won," and the tortoise says, slowly, "There was no fight." Both, somehow, are right. (-14 health)

choices.text: The snake

ok.log: The snake is faster than anything you have ever fought, and it laughs the whole time. You do not win. You do not lose. At the end it coils back round the shell, breathless, and says: "Again. Next winter." The tortoise blinks, as if it had expected exactly this.

fail.deathCause: the snake of the Black Warrior, on a frozen river
fail.log: It was faster than anything you had ever fought.

choices.text: Both

effects.log: "Both," you say. The two heads look at each other a long time. Then they turn, and look each other in the eye, which you understand at once they have never done, and then they look back at you. "Nobody has ever said that," says the snake. "Sit," says the tortoise. You do not fight. You sit on the ice and talk until spring, and it is the hardest bout of your life.

events.text: The next winter you go back to the frozen river, as you promised. The tortoise and the snake are waiting, side by side on the ice, not wound together this time but lying next to each other, the way two old friends sit on a bench. "We thought about what you said," says the snake. "Both," says the tortoise.

choices.text: Ask what they decided

effects.log: "That we are the Black Warrior only when we face each other," the snake says. "Otherwise we are a tortoise and a snake," the tortoise says, "who happen to live together." They wind together again, slowly. When they face each other this time, the ice under you rings like a bell.

choices.text: Ask them to teach you

effects.log: A winter on the ice: from the tortoise, how to stand; from the snake, how to strike; from both, how to choose which, in the moment, without asking. At the end of it you are not stronger. You are, they say, less in two minds.

events.text: A snow goose, a scrap of shell, three words in a slow square hand: Come north. Witness. You go, because you are one of perhaps ten humans under heaven strong enough to make the journey: a month over ice past the last river, to a frozen sea under the aurora, where the northern sky comes down so low you could touch it. In the sky there is an empty seat of black stone among seven stars. On the ice in front of you, a tortoise as big as a hill, a snake round it, the heads turned to face each other.

choices.text: Stand and wait, as a witness does

effects.log: You stand. It takes three days. The tortoise reads its own shell aloud, plate by plate, every ending it ever saw; the snake checks each one for lies, quick and stern. At the end the snake says: "True." The tortoise says: "All of it." And they look up at the empty seat together.

choices.text: Ask why a human should witness this

effects.log: "Because the council will ask," says the snake, "if anybody saw." "And a human," says the tortoise, "lives short enough to tell the truth about it." You think about that the whole three days, standing on the ice.

events.text: The third night. The seven northern stars come down onto the frozen sea like lanterns on a stair, and the tortoise and the snake begin to climb. Halfway up, the snake stops and looks back at you, and asks in its quick dry voice, for the council's record, what you saw.

choices.text: Say: every plate true

effects.log: "Every plate true," you call up into the aurora. The snake nods. The tortoise climbs on. When it reaches the empty seat and settles into it, the whole northern sky turns slowly round it once, like a great wheel coming to rest, and winter, everywhere under heaven, takes a breath.

choices.text: Say what you saw, including the mended crack

effects.log: "Twelve true from the first," you call up, "and one mended. I saw the mending." The snake looks at you for a long time and then, unexpectedly, bows its head. "Better," it says. "The council will believe a mended one." The tortoise takes the seat.

events.text: Years after the night on the frozen sea, every record of every great deed under heaven that you have heard read aloud has had the same odd, careful sound to it, as if each had been checked twice by two very different readers. And one winter morning there is a slate on your desk with your own testimony written on it, word for word, filed.

choices.text: Read it once and put it away

effects.log: It is exactly what you said. Not one word improved. You put it away in a drawer and find, in the following years, that you lie less, even the small lies, as if somebody were keeping your record too.

choices.text: Write back, on the other side of the slate

effects.log: You write: Thank you for letting me see. You leave it in the snow at dusk. In the morning it is gone, and in its place, pressed into the snow, are two marks: a broad square one, and a quick slanting one, side by side.

events.text: A dynasty falls, and the conquerors set its archive on fire: a hall of nine thousand books, the whole memory of a kingdom. You are in the burning hall because you came to save something. Through the smoke, at the far end, on the wet stone floor by a broken cistern, you see a black shell, enormous, perfectly still, and a snake beside it, its head raised. They are not running. They are watching every page burn.

choices.text: Carry out the one book you came for

ok.log: You find it by feel in the smoke, the old law code, and carry it out through the fire with your sleeve over your mouth. On the threshold you look back. The tortoise has not moved. It is witnessing. The snake's head turns to you, and in its look you read: one book, saved; one plate, a little less true. Both of you are right.

fail.log: A beam comes down and you are under it, and the smoke is in your chest, and then something broad lifts the beam off your back from beneath, slowly, as a tortoise lifts its head. You crawl out with the book and nothing else. (-15 health)

choices.text: Stay beside them and watch, and remember

effects.log: You stand beside the shell in the heat and watch every shelf go. You will remember the titles you saw burn for the rest of your life, and, years later, write them down: the list of what was lost, which is itself a kind of book. The tortoise, when the roof falls, turns its head and looks at you, slowly, as one scribe looks at another.

events.text: The new dynasty wants a history of the old one, and has asked you, as one who was there, to help write it. The first chapter the court historians bring you says the last king of the old dynasty burned his own archive in despair. It was the conquerors. You saw it.

choices.text: Refuse to sign it

ok.log: You refuse, publicly, and to your amazement the new emperor lets you rewrite the chapter. It says what you saw. Somewhere in the north, you feel it, a plate on a black shell grows a little brighter.

fail.log: You refuse and are dismissed. The chapter is printed as the court wanted it. But you write your own account and give it to a snow goose, which takes it north, and that account, you are certain, is filed.

choices.text: Sign it, and keep your own true copy hidden

effects.log: You sign, and hide your own version under the floor of your house. It is found centuries later, by a scholar, who is very excited, and who never finds out that a tortoise had the same account on its back all along.

events.text: Autumn equinox, on a deep northern lake. A storm comes down out of a clear sky, from the east, and something long and green and shining dives into the middle of the lake in a single plunge and does not come up. By the first frost the lake is frozen hard, and deep under the clear ice there is a faint green glow, sleeping. And on the ice above it, every night, a black shell with a snake round it lies quite still, as a guard lies across a door.

choices.text: Keep your voice down when you cross the lake

effects.log: You tell the fishermen to cross quietly this winter. They think you are mad, and do it anyway. In spring the ice breaks with a sound like a door, and a long green shape goes up out of the lake into the clouds, without ever looking down at the shell on the shore, which watches it go.

choices.text: Ask the snake who it is guarding

effects.log: "A young one from the east," the snake says. "It dives into our deep every autumn and sleeps. It does not know whose deep it is." "It does not need to," the tortoise says, slowly. "Hush," says the snake. "You will wake it."

events.text: The Azure Dragon of the east, grown great, passes over your hall in a storm of spring rain and stops, which dragons do not do, and asks you a question in a voice like thunder some way off: "You live near the northern lakes. Every autumn I sleep in one of them. Every spring I wake safe. Do you know why?"

choices.text: Tell it about the shell on the ice

effects.log: The storm goes very quiet. "Every winter," the dragon says at last. "For longer than you have lived here. And it never once said." It goes north instead of east. You hear that winter there were two shapes on the ice of the lake, one long and one round, and that the ice did not freeze at all where they lay, because one of them would not stop talking.

choices.text: Say it should ask the north itself

effects.log: "The north," the dragon repeats, and laughs, and goes. You have kept a secret that was not yours, which is the only kind worth keeping. The tortoise, you suspect, would approve. The snake would have told.

events.text: In the Upper Realm a road runs north to seven halls of black ice, each lit by one star: Dipper, Ox, Girl, Emptiness, Rooftop, Encampment, Wall. Seen from far off, the seven together are a tortoise with a snake round it. {npc}, the keeper of the first, a small grave immortal with an ink-stained sleeve, bows. "Each hall keeps one kind of ending," {npc} says. "Lives. Crossings. Marriages. Funerals. Roofs. Armies. Books. The guardian of the north has witnessed ten thousand of each. Would you like to walk them, and read?"
events.arc: The Seven Halls of the North

choices.text: Walk all seven halls

ok.log: It takes you seven years. In the Dipper a register of lives with numbers altered in two hands. In the Ox, bridges and passes and one road home. In the Girl, weddings and partings by rivers. In Emptiness, funerals, ten thousand, each one plain and true. In Rooftop, palaces falling. In Encampment, armies and dykes. In the Wall, heaven's secret books, and among them, very small, your own name. You come out older and lighter, and you know what endings are for.

fail.log: You get through the Dipper and the Ox and stop in the Girl, at a shelf of weddings, because one of them is yours, or should have been, and you cannot read past it. {npc} brings you tea every morning for a year and says nothing at all.

choices.text: Ask {npc} which hall is hardest to keep

effects.log: "Everyone guesses Emptiness," {npc} says. "The funerals. It is not. Funerals are honest. It is the Girl: marriages. Every one of them is two accounts that do not match." {npc} smiles. "The guardian writes them in two columns."

events.text: At the end of the Hall of the Wall, behind the last shelf of heaven's secret books, there is a small cold room with a plain desk, a brush, an inkstone as black as a shell, and a single blank sheet. {npc} says nobody has sat at that desk since the north seat was taken. "The guardian writes on its own back now," {npc} says. "This desk is for a human. If one ever wants it."
events.arc: The Seven Halls of the North

choices.text: Sit, and write one true ending you witnessed

effects.log: You write the death of someone you loved, plainly, the way you saw it. It takes all day. When you finish, the sheet is gone from under your brush, filed, and in its place is a new blank sheet. {npc} nods. "Now there are two clerks," {npc} says. "One slow. One quick. We will see which you are."

choices.text: Leave it blank: it is not yours to fill

effects.log: You leave the room as you found it. {npc} writes something in a ledger. "A refusal," {npc} says, "is also a record. The guardian will like that."

events.text: The Black Tortoise of the Northern Palace sends for you. It lies across the far end of the Hall of the Wall like a black hill, the seven stars on its back, the snake round it reading something off a plate. "You wrote at the desk," says the tortoise. "We read it," says the snake. "One question," they say together. "Was it true?"
events.arc: The Seven Halls of the North

choices.text: Say yes

effects.log: They look at you for a long time, both heads. Then the snake says, "Yes," and the tortoise says, "Yes," and they go back to their reading. That is all. You walk out of the hall feeling as if you had passed the hardest examination of your life by telling the plain truth about one afternoon.

choices.text: Say: as true as I could make it

effects.log: The snake laughs. The tortoise does not. "That," says the tortoise, "is the only honest answer anyone has ever given us to that question." It writes something on a plate of its own back. You will never know what.

events.text: The Northern Palace sends for its human clerk again: the crane whose kingdom fell is before the council at last, and the council wants the hearing's old record read aloud by the one who wrote it. Standing at the long desk in the hall of black ice, you find your old pages waiting, and beside them a new sheet, blank, in case you wish to change anything.

choices.text: Read the old record exactly as written

effects.log: You read it in a level voice. The crane listens with its head bowed. The council of the four directions listens: east, west, south, centre, and the north, where the tortoise sits with the snake round it, both heads still. At the end the Yellow Dragon of the centre says: "Kept." Nobody burns it.

choices.text: Add what you have learned since, in a new column

ok.log: A third column: what came after. The village the crane guards now, where no child drowns. The council hears it. The crane lifts its head. The tortoise and the snake, on the north side, look at each other, and the snake says, quite loudly for a council: "See? An ending is not the end of the record."

fail.log: Your third column wanders, and the Vermilion Bird yawns, and you lose your place. The tortoise, gently, without moving, slides the old pages toward you again with one foot. You read those.

events.text: After the hearing, the snake of the north finds you alone on a terrace of cloud, and coils up on the balustrade beside you like a friend come out for air. "The tortoise wants to know," it says, "whether you would write the council's minutes when it cannot. It is very slow, you see. The Bird burns them before it finishes the first line."

choices.text: Agree, for one season of the council

effects.log: One season. You write fast and the Bird does not catch you once. The White Tiger growls at your shorthand, the Azure Dragon asks for a copy, and the tortoise reads every page afterwards, slowly, and corrects one word in each. You keep the corrected copies all your long life.

choices.text: Say the tortoise should keep its own minutes, slow or not

effects.log: The snake looks at you for a long time. "That is what the tortoise said you would say," it says, aggrieved. "It bet me a fish." It goes off to pay. You find you like the tortoise even more than you thought.

events.text: The Black Emperor of the North, who was once a tortoise and a snake and is now winter itself, asks for an audience. There is a world below the Upper Realm, it says in two voices that have become one, where it is always summer: no winter, no rest, no sleep for the fields or the people, and nothing there ever ends, and so nothing is ever finished. "I cannot go," it says. "If I leave the north, the north forgets to freeze. You are a sovereign. You could carry a winter there."

choices.text: Carry it

effects.log: It breathes once into your cupped hands, and there is a single snowflake there that does not melt. You carry it down for a hundred years. Where you set it on the green world, frost spreads from that spot outward, field by field, and the people of the always-summer stop, and look up, and for the first time in their history, go to bed early.

choices.text: Ask it what it was like to be two

effects.log: "Loud," it says, and one of its voices laughs, the quick one. "We argued for a thousand years. And then, at the very beginning, there was a human who sang down a well, or bought us at a market, or wrote two columns." The slow voice: "We think about that human more than about our whole reign."

choices.text: Decline: a sovereign has a world of their own to keep

effects.log: The Emperor bows both of its heads, which it still has, when it wants to. "That is the right answer for a sovereign," it says, "and the wrong one for a field." It sends someone else. From far off you watch the green world, and see it, after a long while, turn faintly white at the edges, and rest.

events.text: The world you carried winter to has had its first snow, and its people have done what people do: they have invented a solstice festival, and a game for the children in which one of them crawls about under a mat of dry leaves with two heads made of sticks, and the others sing at it: put forth your heads.

choices.text: Go down and watch the game

effects.log: It is badly made and entirely right. The child under the mat puts out one stick head and then the other, and the singers shriek, and you stand at the edge of the village square with the strange feeling that a long story has just started again, somewhere you cannot see.

choices.text: Leave a rice cake on the rim of their well

effects.log: One rice cake on the rim of a well, in the snow. In the morning it is gone. Nothing on this world eats rice cakes. You go back up to the Upper Realm very quietly, smiling.

events.text: On a terrace of cloud you are asked to make up a game of baduk with {npc}, a heavenly immortal you do not know, who laughs easily and plays very fast. Halfway through, setting down a stone, the immortal says: "I was meant to die at nineteen, you know. A monk told me. I took wine up a mountain to two old men at a board like this one." The immortal looks at the board. "Ninety-nine. And then I kept going."

choices.text: Ask who the two old men were

effects.log: "I did not know for a thousand years," the immortal says. "Then I met the guardian of the north at the council, and it nodded at me with both heads, and the snake said: still stealing wine? I nearly fell off my cloud." You laugh so loudly that you lose the game, and do not mind.

choices.text: Play on, and lose gracefully

effects.log: You lose by two stones. The immortal pours the wine. "Ninety-nine was a gift," the immortal says, "but the rest I had to earn." You raise your tea to that. The immortal's wine is good wine, and smells, faintly, of a pine on a mountain long ago.

events.text: {npc}, the immortal who should have died at nineteen, sends you a jar of wine and a note: "Somewhere below there is a child with the same face I had. Nineteen, the monk says. Shall we go up the mountain and sit at the board, you and I, and see what happens?"

choices.text: Go, and take the stern side of the board

effects.log: You sit as the stern one and frown at the board, and {npc} sits as the fair one and smiles, and the child comes up with wine and pours and says nothing. You argue, as the story demands. In the end you take the brush yourself and add the stroke, quick and neat. Ninety-nine. Somewhere in the north, two heads look at each other and are, you are sure, delighted.

choices.text: Say this is the guardian's work, not ours

effects.log: {npc} considers that, and then laughs. "You are right. But I will go up and watch." {npc} goes. Weeks later a note: The two old men came. One sat like a tortoise. The other coiled like a snake. Ninety-nine.

events.text: Winter solstice, the longest night. The river below the village freezes in the dark with a long slow sound, like a breath held, and for a moment the frost on the ice makes a pattern of thirteen great plates, and then it does not.

choices.text: Count the year's endings honestly

effects.log: You sit on the bank and count them: what finished this year, what died, what you let go. You do not decorate them. The cold waits until you have finished, and then the frost on the ice is only frost.

choices.text: Breathe in the north and meditate

effects.log: The north wind at the solstice is thick and slow as river water. You breathe it until the seven stars of the north come out, and go about the next day feeling as if something in you had been set down and steadied, like a stone in a stream.

events.text: A snow goose lands in your courtyard at dawn out of a white sky, walks up to you as if it knew you, and drops at your feet a scrap of black shell, thin as paper, hexagonal. On it, very small, in a slow square hand, is written something you did this year, plainly, exactly as it happened.

choices.text: Read it, and keep it

effects.log: It is not flattering and not cruel. It is simply what happened. You put it in a drawer. In the years that follow, you find you behave a little better in the weeks before the solstice, which you suspect is the point.

choices.text: Give it back to the goose

effects.log: The goose takes it back and looks at you with what you would swear is approval. Records belong to whoever keeps them. It flies north. You feel, oddly, that you have been filed under the honest ones.

events.text: Every winter of your life, on the longest night, you dream the same dream: a council in the sky, four seats and a centre, and you are the one in the north, and you are writing. You never see what you write. You only feel it, on your back, plate by plate, the way you feel a cold wind. You wake each time with your hand cramped as if from a brush.

choices.text: Write down what you remember, each winter

effects.log: A page each winter. Over the years it becomes a strange book: verdicts on rain, on a tiger's ghosts, on a dragon's pride, all in a hand that is yours and is not. You show it to nobody. Once, reading it over, you find a line in a second hand, quick and slanting, that says: Not bad, for a human.

choices.text: Go out and look at the northern stars

effects.log: You stand in the snow and find the seven northern mansions, Dipper to Wall. They look back at you with an expression you recognise, the way you would recognise your own handwriting on an old letter. You go back to bed and sleep without dreaming, for once.

events.text: A case is being heard before the magistrate in your town: two families, one field, two accounts that do not match. The magistrate is lost. You find yourself on your feet in the crowd, without meaning to be, saying: write them down side by side, in two columns, and read where they meet.

choices.text: Go up and do it yourself

ok.log: Two columns on a long sheet, every claim set beside its answer. Halfway down, the two accounts meet in one sentence both families agree with, and the case is over. The magistrate offers you a post as clerk. You find, absurdly, that it is the post you have always wanted.

fail.log: You lose the thread. But the magistrate has seen the idea, and does the two columns himself, slowly, and the case settles. He thanks you. You go home feeling like a clerk who has been too long away from the desk.

choices.text: Sit down again, embarrassed

effects.log: You sit. The magistrate, though, has heard you, and does it, and it works. That night you dream of the council in the sky, and somebody on the east side laughs and says, "It is the north again. It cannot help itself."

events.text: At the council of the Four Guardians, where you have been summoned as a witness on some old matter, the Black Tortoise of the north stops writing when you come in. Both heads turn. The snake says, very quietly, so the others will not hear: "We know that hand."

choices.text: Ask them whose hand it was

effects.log: "Ours," says the tortoise. "Before," says the snake. "You held the brush for a long time," they say together, "and then you let it go to us." You give your testimony, and as you leave the tortoise slides one plate's worth of record across the floor to you: the first verdict you ever wrote, in a life you do not remember.

choices.text: Give your testimony, and say nothing

effects.log: You testify plainly. The tortoise writes it down in a hand you know better than your own. When you have finished it lowers its head to you, both heads, the way a successor bows to the one who held the seat before.

events.text: At a village rite of the five directions, the shaman dances east with a blue fan, south with a red, west with a white, and turns north with the black fan, and stops dead, facing you in the crowd. The candles gutter. The shaman's breath steams. "Winter," the shaman says, in a voice not the shaman's own, "is standing in your yard."

choices.text: Step forward and bow to the north

effects.log: You bow. The cold goes through you like a held breath let out, and you feel, for a moment, every frozen river in the north at once, every sleeper under the ice, every field resting. Then you are only yourself in a crowd, and the shaman is dancing on, and your hands are steady as stone.

choices.text: Laugh it off

effects.log: You laugh, and the crowd laughs with you, and the rite goes on. That winter comes three days after the rite and stays exactly as long as it should, and you find, every morning, frost on your windowsill in the shape of a great slow tortoise lying down.

events.text: A summer of plague, the worst in a generation, and you dream of being winter. In the dream you hold your breath, and the land goes still and white, and the sickness stops. You wake with your lungs aching. The physicians say only a hard cold will end it, and it is midsummer.

choices.text: Go out at night and hold your breath, facing north

ok.log: You stand in the hot dark and hold your breath, and hold it, and something far north holds its breath with you. A frost comes in the night, in midsummer, thin and silver. It kills the fever and half the bean crop. In the morning the town does not know whether to thank heaven or curse it. You do not tell them it was a joint decision.

fail.log: You hold your breath until you faint. Nothing happens. But in the morning, the wind has gone round to the north, and a week later there is a cold rain, and the fevers break. Perhaps it heard you anyway. (-8 health)

choices.text: Tell the physicians to boil water and keep the sick apart

effects.log: It is slower than a frost and harder, and it works, more or less. You learn that a human answer to a winter's question is to do patiently, by hand, what winter would do all at once. The tortoise in you approves. The snake would have frozen it.

events.text: Sheltering from a snowstorm in the northern hills, you crawl into an old grave mound that robbers broke open long ago. Inside, by torchlight, granite slabs, and on each wall a guardian. On the north wall, a black tortoise and a black snake wound round each other, the two heads turned to face each other, so vivid they seem to move in the torchlight. The other walls have faded. This one has not. You know, with your whole body, what it felt like to be poured into that wall.
events.arc: The Tortoise on the North Wall

choices.text: Put your hand on the north wall

effects.log: The stone is cold under your palm, cold as a river in the north. In the dark you hear, or remember, a dying king asking for a guardian, a painter grinding black pigment, and thirteen hundred years of a sleeper breathing in the next room while two heads kept watch on each other. There is a little black on your fingers when you take your hand away.

choices.text: Bow to the sleeper and leave

effects.log: You bow to the coffin platform, as a guard bows going off duty. As you crawl out into the snow you have the absurd feeling that the two heads on the wall turned, for a moment, from each other, and watched you go.

events.text: A scholar of old tombs is going north with a lamp and a copying brush to make a true copy of a tomb mural before the damp takes it, and asks you to come as guard. When you hear which tomb, your hands go cold.
events.arc: The Tortoise on the North Wall

choices.text: Go, and help copy the north wall

effects.log: A month of lamplight in the cold. The scholar copies the faded east and west walls and the ceiling. The north wall you copy, because your hand knows every line of it before the brush moves. The scholar looks at your copy for a long time and says, "You have seen this before." You have. From the inside.

choices.text: Refuse: the sleeper should be left in the dark

effects.log: The scholar goes without you, and comes back with a fine copy of every wall but the north one, which, the scholar says, no lamp would light. The scholar is puzzled. You are not.

events.text: In the same old tomb in the northern hills, by the light of one torch, you stand between two walls you both know from the inside: the north, where a tortoise and a snake face each other, and the west, where a white tiger has flaked away to a neck and a mouth and orange wings. It is the strangest feeling of your life: to be two guardians of one sleeper, in two lives, at once.
events.arc: The Tortoise on the North Wall

choices.text: Touch both walls at once, arms spread

effects.log: Cold stone under one hand, warm stone under the other. For a moment the tomb is full of a slow voice, a quick voice, and a growl like a millstone, all discussing the sleeper's health. Then it is quiet. The sleeper, you are sure, has never been so well guarded.

choices.text: Sit in the middle and keep the watch one night

effects.log: You sit on the cold floor between the walls all night with the torch burning down, a guard of two lives keeping one sleeper. At dawn you crawl out into the snow feeling as if you had stood a very old duty, and stood it well.

events.text: In a grassy field of old royal tombs there is a great stone turtle with its head lifted high, striding forward as if it were glad to be going somewhere, with hexagon plates carved on its back and nothing on top of it: the stele it carried was lost a thousand years ago. Children climb on it. You put your hand on its stone head and feel, with perfect certainty, the weight of a stone that is no longer there.

choices.text: Sit on its back a while, as the children do

effects.log: You sit where the stele should be. The weight lifts off your shoulders, a weight you have carried all your life without knowing what it was. Below you, in the stone, something very slow is, you are almost sure, cheerful.

choices.text: Ask the old tomb keeper what the stele said

effects.log: "Nobody knows," the keeper says. "A king's deeds. They are always the same." The keeper pats the stone head. "But this one remembers. On the anniversary of the king's death, it is warm."

events.text: Ploughing near the old tomb field, a farmer turns up a broken slab of stone with characters on it: a piece of the lost stele. The local magistrate wants to sell it to a collector in the capital. You know where it belongs.

choices.text: Buy it from the magistrate and set it back on the turtle (30 taels)

effects.log: Thirty taels and a cart. You lay the fragment on the stone turtle's back, where the stele once stood. It fits a groove there exactly. The turtle's lifted head, in the evening light, looks, if anything, even more pleased. The children say it smiled.

choices.text: Read the fragment before it goes

effects.log: Three lines: a prisoner in the north, a well, a story about a rabbit. You read them and laugh out loud in the field, and the farmer stares. It is the only fragment of the king's deeds that survives, and it is the only one that mattered.

events.text: There is a stone causeway across a northern river, broad and humped, with plates worn into its surface like a shell's, which the people of the town on the far bank say rose out of the water the night their ancestors fled across it. You cross it for the first time with a bundle on your back, and halfway over your feet know every step.

choices.text: Lie down on it and put your ear to the stone

effects.log: Under your ear, far down, slow, a heartbeat: one beat in the time it takes the river to carry a leaf from bank to bank. Travellers step round you, puzzled. You get up with the strange certainty that you have never been so tired, or so proud, as on the night this stone was a living back.

choices.text: Ask the townsfolk the story

effects.log: Soldiers behind, the river in front, and fish and turtles rising, and one great turtle that did not sink. They tell it every year at the founding festival. You hear it with your eyes shut, and when they get to the part where the soldiers stop at the water's edge, you find your back is aching.

events.text: A spring flood such as the town has not seen in a hundred years. The river is over the causeway, brown and roaring, and on the near bank a crowd of refugees from a burned village behind you, with nowhere else to go. The causeway is under a man's height of water.

choices.text: Wade out onto the causeway first, so they will follow

ok.log: You step onto the drowned stone and it rises under your feet: slowly, broadly, a hand's breadth, then a foot, until its back is out of the flood. The refugees cross behind you in a line, silent, children on shoulders. When the last is over, the causeway sinks back under the water with a sound like a long breath let out.

fail.log: The current knocks you off the stone and you go under, and something under the water carries you back to the bank, slowly, like a hand under a tray. In the morning the flood is down, and the refugees cross, and you watch from the bank with water in your lungs and an odd feeling of having been scolded. (-15 health)

choices.text: Organise the crowd to wait on high ground for the water to fall

effects.log: Two nights on the hill in the rain. On the second, at dawn, the river drops all at once, as if something had stood up beneath it, and the causeway is clear. You lead them over. Halfway, your feet know every step.

events.text: In the south there is a hill shaped like a turtle with its head put forth, where the old kings came down. You climb it at dawn on a whim. At the crown, standing in the hollow where the golden box is said to have landed, you feel the hill under your feet the way you feel your own back: every slope, every stone, as if you had been lying here for a thousand years with your head out, waiting to be sung to.

choices.text: Sing the old song to it

effects.log: "Turtle, turtle, put forth your head." Your own voice, alone on a hill. The ground shivers once, slowly, and then once more, quickly, as if two heads under the earth had both answered and were now arguing about who was asked. You laugh until you have to sit down.

choices.text: Sit in the hollow and look at the valley

effects.log: Fields, villages, a road, a market town: a line of kings came down this hill and all of this is what they made. Some of it is good. You sit there all day, feeling the weight of it on your back, and do not mind the weight.

events.text: A hard age in the south: no rain, no king worth the name, and the descendants of the nine chiefs have climbed the turtle-headed hill again to sing. They have asked you to lead the song, because they have heard you stood on it once and felt it move, and because, they say, the hill shivers when you do.

choices.text: Lead the song

ok.log: Nine villages singing on one hill, and you in the middle with your arms up. The hill shivers, twice, and that evening a rain comes over the valley so gentle that the old people weep. Nobody comes down from the sky in a golden box. But a year later the villages choose a headman, and choose well, and you think perhaps that is what the box always was.

fail.log: You lose the tune and the nine villages lose it with you, and the song falls apart in laughter. The hill shivers anyway, slowly, as if amused. The rain comes three days later.

choices.text: Tell them to stop threatening to roast it

effects.log: "Ask it nicely," you say. The elders look scandalised and then, one by one, amused. They sing it without the roasting. The hill shivers once, very slowly, like an old turtle sighing with relief. The rain comes that night.

events.text: In a naval yard on the southern coast, an old covered warship is drawn up on the slip for repair, spikes on its roof, and at its bow a carved head with a chimney in its throat. A clerk of the yard tells you proudly that it is a dragon's head. You know, the way you know your own face, that it is not.

choices.text: Tell the clerk it is a turtle's head

effects.log: The clerk argues. You point out the plates on the cheeks, the blunt snout, the way the neck comes out of the shell and not out of a body. The clerk looks for a long time and says, slowly, "Huh." It is the most satisfying "huh" you have ever heard.

choices.text: Touch the carved head

effects.log: The wood is warm. You smell sulphur and saltpetre and sea fog, and feel a war's worth of weight on your back, the enemy trying to board and finding nowhere to stand. When you take your hand away, the clerk is staring at you, because the head turned a hair's breadth toward you. Or it did not.

events.text: Pirates on your coast, and a fishing village burning. The only boat at the landing is an old covered barge the villagers built after the pattern of the war ships, clumsy and leaking, with a crude turtle head at its bow. Nobody else knows how to handle it. Your hands do.

choices.text: Take it out against the pirates

ok.log: You take the barge out into the smoke with six fishermen at the oars, and the pirates try to board and find nowhere to stand, and break off. You bring the barge home with the turtle head scorched and the village saved, and you have the feeling, the whole time, of wearing an old coat that fits.

fail.log: The barge is too slow and leaks too much, and you take an arrow in the shoulder. But the pirates, seeing the turtle head come at them out of the smoke, turn and run anyway, as if they remembered something their grandfathers told them. (-16 health)

choices.text: Get the villagers out by land instead

effects.log: You lead them inland through the hills. The village burns. Everyone lives. On the beach, after, you find the old barge still drawn up, untouched, its turtle head turned toward the sea as if it had been keeping watch.

events.text: There is a family in your district whose children always live past nineteen. Always: in the plague years, in the war years, every one. They have a custom nobody else has: on the third day of the third month, the eldest climbs the mountain behind the village with a jar of wine and dried meat, and comes down without them. You are invited to climb with them this year. Your feet know the path.

choices.text: Climb with them, and pour

effects.log: At the top, under a twisted pine, a flat rock with a board scratched into it. Nobody there. The family pours two cups and leaves them. You find yourself sitting down at the board, on the side where the stern one would sit, and frowning at it as if you had a move to make. The family's eldest looks at you very strangely.

choices.text: Ask them why they do it

effects.log: "A debt," the eldest says. "A long time ago one of us should have died at nineteen. Two old men changed the number. One kind, one stern." The eldest looks at you. "You have the stern one's frown, you know."

events.text: A child in the next village is dying of a fever, nineteen years old, and the parents, desperate, have heard that you climb the mountain on the third day of the third month. They bring you a jar of wine and beg.

choices.text: Climb with the wine, and sit at the board yourself

ok.log: You sit at the empty board under the pine and argue with nobody, aloud, for a whole afternoon: the stern side and the fair side, both yourself. At dusk you write, in the air above the board, a nine beside a one. When you come down, the fever has broken. You do not know what you did. A tortoise and a snake would.

fail.log: You sit at the board and nothing comes to you. You come down in the dark, ashamed. The child lives anyway, to fifty, which is not ninety-nine but is not nineteen. Perhaps the old men took it as a partial payment.

choices.text: Send them to a good physician instead, and pay for it (20 taels)

effects.log: Twenty taels to the best physician in the county. The child lives. You climb the mountain anyway on the third day of the third month, with wine, and leave it on the rock, as a thank-you to whoever might be listening.

events.text: You are old now. On the third day of the third month you climb the mountain one last time, very slowly, with a jar of wine. Under the pine there are two old men at the board after all, one fair, one stern, and they look up at you as you come, and both of them smile, which you have never seen the stern one do.

choices.text: Sit down and play

effects.log: You play until dark, three old players at a board for two. You lose. They do not open the book. They do not need to. When you come down the mountain your knees do not ache, and you live, as it turns out, a good long while yet.

choices.text: Pour, and say nothing, as the story says

effects.log: You pour. They drink. At the end the stern one says, "You kept the register well, when it was yours." The fair one says, "Go home." You go home. You do not remember the walk down. You remember the smile.

events.text: On a rock at the edge of the sea, at dawn, sits an old turtle in a small black gauze hat, with a kelp scroll under one foot. It looks at you with immense weariness and some affection, and says, in a voice like the tide going out: "Ah. The minister's old colleague. The palace remembers you. It has a word for you, from the deep."

choices.text: Take the word

effects.log: The kelp unrolls. It says, in the old palace style: The chair by the window on the deep is kept warm. The minister sends regards. The rabbit is still a liar. You laugh until the turtle in the hat sighs, rolls up the scroll, and goes back into the sea.

choices.text: Ask after the palace

effects.log: "The Dragon King is well," the turtle in the hat says, "and still cannot eat liver. The fish ministers still quarrel. Your chair is still by the window." It looks at you. "You were very good at sitting in it."

events.text: A fishing village asks you to settle a dispute with the sea: three boats lost in a month, and they mean to stop fishing the bay altogether. You walk down to the shore at dusk, and find you know, without knowing how, exactly the phrasing the palace under the sea likes to be addressed in.

choices.text: Speak to the sea in the old court style

effects.log: Formal, slow, with all the honorifics: a humble petition from the people of the shore to His Majesty of the Deep. The waves stop for a breath. In the morning a turtle in a black hat leaves a kelp scroll on the beach that says: A misunderstanding with an eel. Resolved. No more boats are lost.

choices.text: Tell the village to fish further out, where it is safe

effects.log: Practical, and it works. But at dusk you go down alone and apologise to the sea anyway, in the old style, for the trouble. The tide comes in very gently that night, as if somebody under it were mollified.

events.text: You have taken work at the royal ice house by the palace, carrying blocks out into the summer for the king, the officials, the sick and the old. The other workers say this ice house is a wonder: in a hundred years it has never once run out, not even in the warm winters. Going down into the dark of it for the first time, your feet know every step, and under the floor, under the ice, you feel something lying very still, keeping cold.
events.arc: The Ice That Never Runs Out

choices.text: Kneel on the cold floor and put your palms flat on it

effects.log: Under your palms, far down, a slow heartbeat, one beat a winter. Cold comes up through your hands like a greeting from an old friend who does not get many visitors. When you stand, the other workers are watching, and one of them, very old, nods as if this had happened before.

choices.text: Carry the first block to the sick ward, not the palace

effects.log: Against orders. The overseer shouts, then sees where you are going, and stops shouting. The block goes into the fever ward and the room cools like an evening. That night you dream of lying in the dark under a great weight of ice, and being glad of every block that goes to the ward.

events.text: A cruel minister wants the ice house's whole stock for a summer banquet, every block, the sick ward's share and all. The order comes down. The overseer looks at you, because everyone knows the ice behaves differently when you are in the house.
events.arc: The Ice That Never Runs Out

choices.text: Lock the ice house and refuse

ok.log: You stand in the doorway and refuse, and the minister's men find, to their bewilderment, that the cold coming out of the door is too bitter to walk into. The banquet is held without ice. The sick ward gets its share. You are not punished; somebody higher up has decided not to know about it.

fail.log: You are dragged out of the doorway and beaten. The minister's men go in for the ice. They come out with half of it: the rest, they say, would not come loose from the floor. The sick ward gets that half. (-10 health)

choices.text: Send the ice, but send the sick ward's share first, by night

effects.log: You carry the ward's blocks out at midnight. In the morning the minister's men take the rest. That summer, oddly, the ice house's stock lasts until the first frost anyway, as if somebody under the floor had quietly made more.

events.text: There is an old turtle in the mill pond below the village, plain and brown and very ordinary, which the children feed and the miller swears has been there since his grandfather's time. You sit on the bank and look at it, and it looks at you, and you feel, for no reason, the exact shape of something missing: a coil round your back that is not there, a second voice that has stopped answering.

choices.text: Sit with it a while every evening

effects.log: Every evening that summer. It does not do anything. It sits on its log in the last sun. You find the missing thing aches less when you sit with something that is missing the same thing. By autumn it swims over to your side of the pond when you come.

choices.text: Feed it and go home

effects.log: You give it a crust. It eats it slowly. When you go, you look back once, and it is watching the stream that comes down into the pond from the hills, upstream, as if expecting someone.

events.text: Hunting in the high hills above the mill pond, you come to a deep pool under a waterfall where the old people say a great serpent has been waiting a thousand years to become a dragon. Something long and black lies at the bottom, very still. As you lean over the water it lifts its head and looks at you, and you both know each other.

choices.text: Tell it about the old turtle in the mill pond

effects.log: It listens to the end. Then it lies a long while with its chin on the stones at the pool's edge. "I did not look back," it says at last. "I thought if I looked back I would not go." It looks down the valley, toward the mill pond, for the first time in a long time. You leave it looking.

choices.text: Ask it whether it became what it wanted

effects.log: "Not yet," it says. "A thousand years. It is slow without the slow one." It almost laughs. "It was always the patient one. I only knew how to want." You go down the hill and, passing the mill pond, tell the old turtle, for no reason, that it is missed.

events.text: On the riverbank below the village there is a rock shaped exactly like a turtle drawn into its shell, and at the New Year the village ties a straw rope round it with white paper strips, sets out rice and a cup, and bows. They call it Turtle Rock. When it is your turn to bow, you cannot. You stand there with the strangest feeling that you are bowing to yourself.

choices.text: Bow anyway, the deepest bow you can

effects.log: You bow to the ground. As your forehead touches the frozen earth you feel the rock as if from inside: dark, quiet, and waiting, with a long thin ache along one side where something used to lie coiled. You stand up with wet eyes. The old people nod as if this were normal. Perhaps it is.

choices.text: Put your hand on the rock instead

effects.log: Cold stone, and under it, very slow, something that is not quite asleep. Along its back runs a groove you never noticed, thin and curving, like the place where a snake once lay. You trace it with one finger, all the way round.

events.text: A road is being built along the river, and the magistrate's engineers mean to break up Turtle Rock for the foundations. The village is in uproar. The engineers have hammers. You have, for some reason, the deep certainty that the rock is not quite finished waiting.

choices.text: Stand on the rock and refuse to move

ok.log: You stand on it for three days in the snow. The village brings you food. On the third day the engineer in charge gives up and moves the road ten paces inland. That night, alone, you hear the rock make a sound like a long slow breath in its sleep.

fail.log: They pull you off and swing a hammer. The hammer breaks. So does the second. The engineers move the road inland, muttering about bad stone. You nurse your bruises and grin. (-10 health)

choices.text: Petition the magistrate with the whole village

effects.log: A hundred signatures, two hundred bows, a basket of persimmons. The magistrate moves the road. Turtle Rock stays. At the next New Year, when you bow, you feel, very far down, something turn over in its sleep and settle again, content.

events.text: A sect auction in a lantern-lit hall. The last lot comes out on black lacquer: a great black shell, thirteen plates, cracked from end to end by fire, the cracks fine as hair. The auctioneer says it was a dynasty's oracle for two hundred years and that every reading taken from it came true. Every crack on it aches in your own back as you look at it.

choices.text: Bid for it, whatever it costs (300 taels)

effects.log: Three hundred taels, and the room hates you. When it is carried to you, every ache in your back stops at once, the way a child stops crying when it is picked up.

choices.text: Stand up and tell them what it was

ok.log: You tell them: two heads, one shell, a river, the diviners' hunt, two hundred years over a brazier. You do not know how you know. The room goes very quiet. Nobody bids. The sect elder brings the shell to you on its lacquer tray and leaves without a word.

fail.log: They laugh you out of the hall. The shell goes to a great family for four hundred taels. You hear the next year that they heated it to ask about a marriage, and it said no, and was right.

choices.text: Leave: you cannot breathe here

effects.log: Outside, in the cold, you breathe until your back stops hurting. Through the paper doors you hear the gavel. You never ask who bought it.

events.text: The cracked shell sits in your room. On winter nights, if you put your hand on it, you can feel the cracks moving, very slightly, as if they were trying to say one more thing. It has taken you years to decide what to do with it.

choices.text: Ask it one question, without heating it

ok.log: You ask, aloud, whether it wants to go home. The cracks move under your palm, all of them, slowly, into one long line from end to end, north to south. In the old books that means a road. You understand.

fail.log: The cracks do not move. Perhaps it is tired of being asked things. You sit with your hand on it all night anyway, asking nothing, and in the morning you feel better, and you think, so does it.

choices.text: Carry it north and give it to the river

effects.log: A month north on foot. On the ice of a cold river you set it down. The ice opens under it, slowly, like a mouth, and it sinks, and for a moment, under the clear water, you see two heads come out of it, one slow, one quick, and look at each other, and then there is only the river.

choices.text: Bury it under the oldest pine you can find

effects.log: You dig until your hands bleed, and lay it in, and fill it. A snow goose watches the whole time from a branch, and when you have finished it calls once, not unkindly, and flies off north to tell somebody.

events.text: A court diviner heats a turtle plastron in the town square to read the year for the king. You stand in the crowd. As the bone cracks in the fire, you feel it across your own back, a line of heat from shoulder to hip, and you have to sit down in the dust.

choices.text: Tell the diviner what the cracks say before the diviner can

effects.log: You read it aloud from the ground, every line, without looking at the bone. The diviner goes pale, checks, and finds you right in every particular. The square falls silent. You get up and walk away and are sick behind the well. Some knowledge is paid for twice.

choices.text: Get up and leave the square

effects.log: You leave. The heat in your back fades as you go. You never again stand near a brazier, and on the day, years later, that the court stops reading shells, you go down to the river and sit there for a long time, and are glad.

events.text: All your life you have been unable to tell even a small lie without feeling it, physically, as a hairline crack somewhere across your back. White lies to a host, a softened report to a superior: each one a crack, and each one aches in the frost. People think you are honest. You are not, especially. You are only in pain when you are not.

choices.text: Go a whole year without a single lie

ok.log: A year. It costs you two friends and a post, and gains you three friends and a better post. At the end of it your back does not ache in the frost for the first time in your life, and you sleep a whole winter night through.

fail.log: You last until the spring, when you tell a dying old neighbour that the harvest will be good. It is a lie. It cracks across your back like ice. You find you do not regret it, and the crack, oddly, does not ache.

choices.text: Find out what the old crack under your shoulder is from

effects.log: The oldest one, the one that has always been there. A shaman puts her hand on it and goes very quiet, and says only: "Something you wrote, once, that you did not see. Before this life." She will not take your money.

events.text: In the Upper Realm, at the northern edge of heaven, there is an empty seat of dark stone among seven stars, and cracked tablets lie at its foot that nobody has cleared away. You stand before it and know every crack on every tablet. The seat has been empty for an age because of you.

choices.text: Pick up the tablets and mend them, one by one

effects.log: It takes a century. For each crack you go down to the world below and find the place and the truth. At the end, thirteen tablets, whole, stacked by the seat. Nobody sits in it. But the next time the council meets, there is a clerk again, a young tortoise with a thread of black snake round it, writing very slowly, and checking twice.

choices.text: Sit in the seat yourself, once, and stand up again

effects.log: Cold stone. You sit for the space of one breath and feel the whole weight of the north settle on you and find you wanting. You stand. It is not yours, and was not, the last time either. You leave it empty and honest, which is better than full and false.

events.text: Walking a cold river in the north in the first frost, you come to a bank of black sand and stop, because your feet will not go on. You kneel and brush the sand with your hand, without knowing why, and there, a finger's depth down, is an egg: dark, cool, faintly warm at the heart. You put your palm on it. Two heartbeats, out of time with each other, slow and quick.

choices.text: Cover it again gently and keep the frost off it

effects.log: You heap the black sand back over it and lay your cloak on top against the frost and sit beside it until dawn. When you take the cloak back, there is a print in the sand under it, small, like a shell, and a thin curving line beside it, like a thread.

choices.text: Sit with it and tell it everything you remember

effects.log: You do not know what you remember until you start: a well, a basket, a frozen river, a council, a brush. You talk until the sun is up. The two heartbeats, by the end, have fallen into step. You think that is a good sign.

events.text: Years after the black sand you go back to the river in the north. The egg is gone. In the shallows by the bank, palm-sized, a black hatchling with a thread of black snake round it is trying to decide which way the water is, and the two heads are arguing about it.

choices.text: Point downstream

effects.log: The tortoise head looks where you point. The snake head looks the other way, on principle. Then both of them look at you, for a long moment, as if they had seen you before, and turn downstream together, slowly, and go.

choices.text: Say nothing, and let them decide

effects.log: You sit on the bank and let them argue. It takes all morning. In the end they go upstream a little, and then downstream, and then, for no reason you can see, into the deep middle of the river, both heads agreed. You walk home feeling that you have watched the first page of something very long.
